en: The reality of Brahman is of the nature of dense bliss and awakening, incomparable, liberated from the limits of time and space, eternally free, and manifested by hundreds of thousands of Vedic scriptures; though indistinct when merely perceived, it consists of the great goal of human existence.
Alas, that very reality shines forth directly in the city of the Guru’s breath; such is the good fortune of people!

Thus, regarding even that which is difficult to obtain, people— alas!— clearly manifest their meanness by treating it as easily attained and already in hand, honoring it instead with body, speech, or mind;
whereas we, for our part, shall strive with a most steadfast mind to eliminate the suffering of the entire world.
We take refuge in this very Lord of the City of the Wind (Kāñcī), who is the soul of all without exception.
That *sattva* which was previously stainless due to its lack of conditioning by the [other] two [guṇas],
by means of that [sattva]— which, through the sleep of the elements (*bhūtanidrā*), consists of the body— it is heard repeatedly in the words of Vyāsa that "this is the body.
Because of its transparency, it has a form consisting of the unobscured radiance of the consciousness that is the bliss of the Supreme.
In that body of yours, which is sweet with learning and wisdom and easy to grasp, the fortunate ones delight.

In the stainless ocean of Brahman— which is unwavering, eternally full, infinite, consisting of the nectar of supreme bliss, and most beautiful with the many strings of liberated souls merged within it—
they say that the self is indeed the exceedingly pure *sattva*, comparable to the surging of its waves.
O Infinite One, why do we say that You, who are partless, are "with parts" (sakala), if it is only in Your own kalās?

O Unborn One! Although You are devoid of activity and without motive, because You engage in the action called "Beholding," the latent primordial nature (*prakṛti*)—though unreal and like a mere illusion—arises at the beginning of a kalpa.
From that [nature], a certain perfectly pure portion, which is of the nature of *sattva* and free from obscuration, [emerges].
O Vaikuṇṭha, O You whose power and majesty are unimpeded, You maintain Your own form by sustaining it Yourself.
May that [face] of yours— which performs the playful sport of a row of lovely kalāya flowers held by fresh rain-clouds,
which is the singular essence of loveliness, the descent of full merit for the eyes of virtuous people,
the fearless abode of Lakṣmī’s play, and an internal outpouring of nectar— [protect me].
O Lord of the Abode of Maruts, sprinkle the bodies of those who contemplate [you], and may I perceive them!

O Unconquered One! Previously, I considered that your creative activity was painful for living beings, bringing about excessive weariness with worldly existence; yet today I do not perceive it as such. Otherwise, how could these living beings [be so uplifted by] this body of yours, which is most harmonious and moistened with the essence of consciousness?
Having drunk with their eyes and ears from the flood of the ocean of the nectar of supreme rasa, they shall rejoice.

O Hari! You are the Pārijāta tree, obtainable by all without exception and yielding infinite fruit; for those who bow before you, you constantly place [your presence] ever before them, bestow even those objects and desires not requested, and grant a state dense with supreme bliss. Thus, you are the one from whom everything can be obtained.
This multitude of supplicants vainly longs for that insignificant tree of Śakra’s grove.

Out of compassion, others indeed give away other objects of desire, but you are a giver of your own self; you are distinguished by this, for while others rule over the world through sovereignty and the like, you are the lord even of yourself.
Those of abundant fortune find great delight in you at every step, for you are sweet to the mind. You are [the Supreme].
O Śauri, who delights even in the Self and who is the receptacle of an immeasurable multitude of virtues—salutations to You!

Sovereignty consisting in the subjugation of Śaṅkara and other lords; prowess that withdraws the splendor of those who steal the world’s luster; and stainless fame sung even by those free from desire;
the Goddess Śrī is ever attached to your limbs, yet there is no report of your attachment to anything anywhere.
O dweller in the temple of the wind, O slayer of Mura! You are the primary refuge for the word "Bhagavat."
His forehead is illuminated by a tilaka rising above a crown that rivals the sun;

his eyes are agitated with compassion and his smile is radiant with tenderness; his nostrils are well-formed, and his cheeks are adorned with a pair of shark-shaped earrings, while his neck shines with the Kaustubha gem.
I worship Your form, radiant with a forest garland, a serpent-hood, and the Śrīvatsa mark.

I take refuge in that form of yours which destroys all suffering—Your four glorious arms adorned with armlets, bracelets, bangles, and excellent great-jewel rings, holding a mace, a conch, a discus, and a lotus; and which clings to shimmering yellow garments that conceal Your golden waist, while Your feet possess the luster of stainless lotuses.

Your form is more enchanting than that which deludes even the great ones of the three worlds; it is more beautiful than the repository of loveliness itself; it is sweeter than the very pinnacle of sweetness;
it is more beautiful than the supreme of beauty; and it is more wondrous than the most marvelous of wonders.
O pervasive Viṣṇu! in this world, who does not nourish a sense of wonder?

Having attained Your body, which is of such a sweet nature, that Goddess—who is composed of the essence of bliss—does not remain for even a moment, even among her own devotees, due to her supreme longing.

Alas, O Acyuta! O All-pervading Lord! because of the power of the steadiness of her love for the beauty of Your form, and through the force of her lack of fickleness, the very report of her fickleness has arisen as a source of distress for her.
O Lord of Lakṣmī! This Lakṣmī herself has surely been captivated by the beauty of Your hands, for she is unstable when it comes to others; now I shall state another proof as well:
those people who are devoted to the nectar of chanting the qualities of Your feet are indeed true devotees.
Among them, she dwells with constant stability, her attention fixed upon the mention of her beloved.

Your form— which consists of the elixir of supreme consciousness, which is the extraction of the essence flowing from the earth of such lovely qualities, and which captivates the hearts of those who hear it—
immediately impels the intellect, intoxicates the mind, and causes the limbs to bristle with joy.
He also drenches [her] with streams of cold tears born from a swoon of joy.
For this very reason, yoga expressed as devotion is proclaimed by the lords of yogis to be far more excellent than the two other forms of yoga consisting of action and knowledge;
indeed, toward You, whose essence is the singular flavor of beauty, there exists the nature of the highest intensity of love.
O Beloved of Ramā! Devotion alone is easily attainable by all people in the world.
That which is called *karmayoga*— the performance of one’s own duty with self-restraint and free from desire—
is far inferior; whereas that which is to be attained through the knowledge of the Upaniṣads is even more difficult for the mind to grasp because of its unmanifest nature, O All-pervading Lord!
Devotion consisting of love for you alone is eternally your own and most excellent.

Having performed ritual actions that cause excessive exertion, those purified of impurities reach a state of expansion on the path of devotion to Awakening—or even on the path of logic; what does it matter?
Others, however, having exhausted themselves on the path of logic, [seek] your supreme body known as Brahman.
Apart from softness of mind, even with much reflection, they succeed only after many future births.

But devotion to you, O Lord, is victorious; by immersing oneself in the stream of the nectar of the rasa of your stories, it spontaneously accomplishes itself, effortlessly extending the path of pure awakening. It grants immediate perfection—may that very devotion be mine unto your feet.
O Lord of the abode of the wind, may the moistness of the essence of mature love flow forth most swiftly!
O Giver of Boons! Those devotees who, reciting Your names, fall into the ocean of the weight of their joy; who, remembering Your form, become eloquent in praising Your virtues;
and who, practicing [devotion], truly delight in the Supreme—[they alone find true rest].
I do not consider those who have attained all their desires to be truly fortunate.
O Viṣṇu, alas! Your mind remains unattached even to the abundance of the nectar of serving Your feet; it is afflicted and distressed—have mercy!
[For one who] relishes the nectar of remembering Your lotus-feet and [repeats] the multitude of Your names...
I shall not dwell anywhere in solitude, singing my own praises.
If compassion has arisen within you, what indeed is unattainable for embodied beings?
What is this state called "the pacification of the flood of my afflictions" compared to it? Who in this world is not constantly afflicted by grief?
Your devotees, being liberated and unattached, attain a state of happiness.

O Lord! Indeed, those sages— Nārada and others, whose internal states are profound and hidden from the world, who have become mature in wisdom, and who are free from all pain through the remembrance of Your lotus feet— wander at their own will, having eternally manifested the supreme consciousness within themselves.
What else remains for those who are completely immersed in the expansion of eternal bliss and non-duality?
May my devotion to you flourish; that alone shall pacify the entire flood of my afflictions— of this there is not even a grain of doubt in my heart,
provided it is not contradicted by the words of Vyāsa, your own speech, or the words of the Vedas.
Everything would become false, consisting for the most part of the mere words of men on the street.
Devotion to you is sweet from the very beginning through the flavor of your virtues;
if it ascends even to me, it will pacify all afflictions,
and finally, at the end, it will meet with the arising of pure, perfect enlightenment within my own mind.
It bestows the non-duality of great bliss; what else remains to be sought?
Having shaken off my afflictions, make Your pair of feet full of nectar for me upon reaching Your sacred field; likewise, grant Your hand for the rite of worship,
Your eye for beholding Your form, and Your tulasī from Your feet—
O you of beautiful conduct, your sense of smell is for smelling [the fragrance of virtue], and your hearing is likewise [for hearing the Dharma].
When my heart was forcibly overwhelmed by abundant mental anguish and physical disease,
may that form of yours— whose nature is supreme aesthetic bliss and pure consciousness— arise within it;
[a state] in which the hair on my body stands on end and a flood of tears of intense joy flows forth.
Just as you might forget a suffering that is difficult to pacify and full of humiliation.
O Lord of Marudgṛha! Even those who are hostile toward you surely become happy; yet I, who am devoted to you, suffer greatly—what is this?
O Giver of Boons, let there be no infamy for you as you pacify this burden of my speech.
O subduer of Kaṃsa, quickly make me the crest-jewel of Your devotees!
O Lord, what is the use of further words? For as long as compassion arises within you,
I shall spend my days before you, O Giver of Boons, having placed my feet upon your prepared pedestal, while uttering various cries of distress sent forth by me.
To the best of one's ability, one should clearly perform prostrations, praises, and service.
Grant me such health as may make me fit for the service of you;
through the eightfold practice of yoga clearly perfected, may I quickly attain your satisfaction.
Purified by restraints such as firmness in celibacy and observances such as ritual bathing,
we, devoted solely to you, shall firmly assume the lotus posture or any other suitable seat.
Constantly contemplating the syllable *Tāra* within and restraining the vital breath, we remain pure,
having withdrawn our senses from their objects and being intent upon the worship of you.
While our physical forms remain unmanifest, let us repeatedly and with effort fix our intellects upon You;
by that means, contemplating Your feet, may we bear within us the nectar of devotion.

Devoted to the yoga of meditation and taking refuge in you, we contemplate your body— beautiful with its clearly manifested distinct parts— in our minds without effort, by virtue of long-term cultivation.

O Mother! For those who meditate upon Your entire form—such as it is—and whose souls are captivated by its unfolding sweetness, the internal Brahman, whose nature is identical to the dense nectar within, shines forth.
O Leader of the Universe, having taken refuge in that state consisting of your meditative absorption, which takes the form of relishing that [bliss],
we shall, upon emerging from it, again undertake the practice of *dhāraṇā* and the other stages.
Thus, with our hearts overflowing through the intensity of practice and celebrating the festival of the supreme Self,
may we attain the status of crowns upon the heads of the assembly of liberated devotees, wandering like Śuka, Nārada, and others.
But as for one who, desiring liberation either quickly or gradually, seeks victory in your samādhi, O Unborn One— he,
by means of yoga, slowly raises the vital breath, which is brought under control, through the *suṣumṇā* by means of the six supports.
Then, even casting off the subtle body (liṅgadeha), he who is free from worldly attachment merges into you, the Supreme;
however, one who is curious about the higher worlds departs through the crown of the head together with the sense organs.

Having reached the station of the Sun by means of the fires, days, lunar mansions, fortnights, and the deities presiding over them during the northern solstice, you, devoted to Bhava, shall proceed joyfully as far as the station of Dhruva.
When he, established in the great abode, is afflicted by the heat from the fire of Śeṣa’s mouth,
he then goes to your refuge, or rather, even before that, to the station of Brahmā.
Whether dwelling there or in your own abode, one attains liberation at the time of the elemental dissolution;
indeed, by his own will, he may even be liberated beforehand, having forcibly shattered the cosmic egg of the universe.

O Lord! Entering that [Self] by means of its respective natures—the seven coverings consisting of earth, water, fire, air, ether, the intellect (*mahat*), and primordial nature (*prakṛti*)—the one who is at peace attains Your unconditioned state.

O Lord of the Universe! O You whose nature is Being-Consciousness-Bliss! Moving along such a path beginning with light, one does not suffer a fall; O Lord of the Wind, protect me as I utter the rising qualities of Your majesty!
Before the dissolution of primordial matter, this world— both manifest and unmanifest— became nothing at all;
having entered into you, who abide in Māyā where the equilibrium of the *guṇas* has suppressed all modification,
there was then neither death nor immortality, and no state of day or night.
There, indeed, you alone shall subsist by means of the nature of the light of supreme bliss.

O All-pervading Lord! When You, having attained the delight of the play of consciousness, entered into dissolution, Time, Karma, the qualities (guṇas), the multitudes of individual souls, and the entire universe of effects likewise became absorbed within You.
O Lord! Those who abide as Your very essence through Your power do not at all declare them to be non-existent.
If not, how could there be a further arising of things that are like flowers in the sky?
And so, when you, having passed through two *parārdhas* of time, bore within yourself the desire to create, Māyā herself manifested for the sake of bringing the three worlds into being;
indeed, from Māyā arise the power of Time (*kāla-śakti*), all unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa*), and even inherent nature (*svabhāva*).
Having manifested and displayed their qualities, they rendered her assistance.

You are celebrated as the Witness, present within Māyā yet not having entered its body; and when You have entered it through reflection by means of various distinctions, You are the Jīva, who is indeed not other than Yourself.
Then, awakened by Time and other factors, and impelled by You Yourself—
That Māyā indeed created the principle of intellect (buddhi-tattva), which is called the Great One (mahat).

In that regard, although the Great Principle (Mahat) consists of the three *guṇas*, it is predominantly *sattva* and indeed produces the non-conceptual "I-consciousness" (*ahaṃkāra*) within this individual soul (*jīva*).
Within this wheel, the Great Principle is indeed the principle of the "I" (*ahaṃtattva*) which brings about conceptual awareness.
O Viṣṇu, by Your impulsion, it becomes fully nourished by the three qualities and exceedingly abundant in darkness (tamas).
Thus, having attained a threefold state through the sequence of the three qualities (guṇas), I became the Vaikārika [ego],
which further becomes Taijasa and Tāmasa; first, by means of that ego whose nature is Sattva,
I created the gods who pride themselves on their senses, as well as the quarters, the wind, the sun, Pāśī, and the Aśvins.
Vahni, Indra, Acyuta, Mitra, Kā, Vidhu, Vidhi, Śrī, Rudra, and Śārīraka.

O All-pervading One! By Your power, that internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa)—which consists of the functions known as mind (manas), intellect (buddhi), ego (ahaṅkāra), and consciousness (citta) combined together—emitted only the portions of *sattva*.
From the *taijasa* [aspect] was born the group of ten organs, and furthermore, from the *tāmasa* portion...
O Lord of the City of the Wind! By your power, the sound was produced from a mere fragment of the ether.
From sound, O All-pervading Lord, you then created touch; from that, the wind; from that, form; from that, light; then taste and water; and smell and earth.
Thus, O Mādhava, through the successive addition of each preceding element, each subsequent one is endowed with the qualities of its predecessors.
O Blessed One, you alone have revealed this multitude of beings from the state of darkness.
These hosts of elements, as well as the hosts of senses and the gods, having been born separately, were then unable, even with these deities, to perform the act of fashioning the cosmic egg;
you, whose qualities are praised by various hymns, entered into those principles.
Having proclaimed their inability to act, you fashioned those golden orbs by weaving them together.
That egg indeed remained for a thousand years in the waters created previously;
without becoming weary, You fashioned it into the form of the fourteen worlds known as Virāṭ,
consisting of all individual souls, with thousands of hands, feet, and heads.
O Lord of the City of the Maruts, you have appeared; protect me from every disease!
O Lord! Thus, for You who have become the very nature of the fourteen worlds, they say that the sole of Your foot is Pātāla,
and even the region above Your foot, O God, is Rasātala.
O you of wondrous nature, the two ankles are indeed the Mahātala region.
O Lord! Your two calves are Talātala and Sutala; Your pair of knees are Vitala and Tala;
Your hips are Kṣoṇītala, and Your navel is the sky.
And your chest, O wielder of the discus, is the abode of Śakra!
Your neck is the Maharloka, your face Janaloka and Tapoloka,
and your forehead is Satyaloka, the totality of the universe— O You who consist of the world! By those who have taken refuge in the world...
O Blessed One, salutations to you whose body is bound by others!
O Lord! Your cranial aperture is the abode; O Keśava! the meters are the roots of the universe, and your locks of hair are the clouds;
the pair of your shimmering eyes is the dwelling place of Brahmā.
The eyelashes are night and day, and the sun is the eyes.
O Blessed One, the entire creation of the universe is the casting of Your sidelong glances;
the two ears are the quarters of space, the two nostrils are the pair of Aśvins,
and greed and shame are Your lower and upper lips.
The clusters of stars are her teeth, and Yama is her fangs.
O Lord! Your illusory power is the playful smile, Your breath is the wind, Your tongue is the water, and Your speech is the flight of birds;
the Siddhas and other celestial hosts are the cavities of Your mouth, and fire is the opening of Your nostrils.
The gods are your arms, and the god Dharma is the pair of your breasts.
O Lord! Your back is the Unrighteousness (Adharma) here; O lotus-eyed one, Your mind is the moon, and Your heart-lotus is the Unmanifest (Avyakta).
Your belly is the multitude of oceans, and Your garment is the two twilights (Sandhyā).
The penis is Prajāpati, and Mitra is in the two testicles.
The hosts of deer are her hips; the nails on her feet are elephants, camels, and horses; Time itself is her gait;
and the abodes of the Brahmin and other castes are her lotus-face and arms.
O Ocean of Compassion, [I bow] to Your pair of beautiful thighs and feet!
O Wielder of the Wheel, the wheel of saṃsāra is your illusion; your activity is the wheel, your vigor is the host of great asuras, the bones are the mountains,
the channels are the gathering of rivers, and the body hairs are the trees.
May this ineffable form of the Lord be victorious!
They say that such a body of yours, consisting of the entire universe, should be remembered by those who partake in karma at the time of the exhaustion of their karma;
for you, whose inner self is a stainless mind, [this is the true form].
O Lord of the abode of wind! Homage be to you; ward off all diseases.
"So be it, O Lord! Having first arisen in the form of the fourteen-fold world,
you have now indeed been born above that as the Creator himself within the assembly of Satyaloka—
whom they praise as Hiraṇyagarbha, the life-soul of the entire three worlds."
He who existed with the essence of a manifold desire to create, blossoming through the transformation of abundant passion.
Having set his heart upon the creation of the universe, he remained there, agitated by anxiety, for he had not yet attained the self-evident realization regarding the nature of the world;
at that moment, O Lord of the worlds, a voice from the sky cried out, "Perform penance! Perform penance!"
We have heard this speech of his, which is pleasing to the ear and provides an impetus toward asceticism.
"Who was that man who spoke to me?"— thus did you reflect on the meaning of those words while gazing in all directions through the world-mandala filled with water, seeing nothing at all;
by him, who had undertaken such asceticism for a thousand divine years, were you propitiated.
To him, you have shown your own abode, Vaikuṇṭha, which is uniquely marvelous.
Where Māyā never manifests her transformations, where the world appears externally yet remains transcendent, and where states such as sorrow, anger, delusion, and fear have gone far away;
there, within that nature which is the radiance of the supreme light, flows a dense torrent of bliss.
That abode of Yours, manifested as the form of Vaikuṇṭha, reigns supreme, O All-pervading Lord!
In that [world], celestial beings shine forth— four-armed, with complexions as dark as sapphire yet radiant as gold,
illuminating the quarters with the light of various jeweled ornaments, dwelling in royal celestial palaces,
and having attained such exalted stations through their devotion.
May that abode of yours, which has cast off all impurity and takes the form of Vaikuṇṭha, be victorious!
Surrounded by various celestial women, and illuminating the quarters of the sky with her creeper-like body— charming and intoxicating to the whole world— which resembles a flash of lightning,
Lakṣmī herself is perceived out of her singular curiosity for the fragrance of your lotus feet.
Grant me that state of yours, which possesses such wondrous and divine majesty.
There, when his own station had been thus revealed, [he beheld] the Cause, seated upon a jeweled throne,
his form radiant with ornaments such as a crown and bracelets brilliant like ten million suns,
marked with the Śrīvatsa, and reddened by the luster of the Kaustubha gem he wore.
O All-pervading Lord, may that form of Yours which Brahmā beheld among all things shine forth within me!
He whose splendor is as soft as a dark rain cloud or a fresh jasmine bud; who covers the circle of the directions with his discus;
whose noble face is brightened by the flow of a broad, gentle smile;
and whose glorious circle of arms bears the shining conch, mace, sword, and lotus.
O All-pervading Lord, may this form of yours, which brings satisfaction to the Creator, dispel my disease.
Upon seeing you, the Lotus-born Brahmā, filled with intense agitation and overcome by a surge of joy, fell at your lotus-feet, feeling fulfilled through his love;
O Lord, you already know my desire— grant me that knowledge!
I worship You, who declare that Your own nature is supreme, consisting of both duality and non-duality.
Then, touching his copper-hued feet with his hand as he bowed low, [the Lord] spoke these words:
"Your awakening shall come to pass; even bondage does not arise through the processes of creation.
Having thus spoken and greatly gladdened him, he himself remained hidden within that man's mind.
O Blessed One, you raised him up at the time of creation; may he, being uplifted, manifest his vigor.
Thus, at the end of the dissolution of the primordial matter, having obtained birth for the first time in the Brahma-kalpa,
Brahmā received the Vedas from you once again and carried out the creation of beings similar to those of the previous kalpa.
Thus he has passed many times through days measured by a thousand cycles of four yugas and nights of equal duration; now, having dissolved together with all his own creations, he sleeps within you.
Therefore, they call his night the occasional dissolution (naimittikapralaya).
Furthermore, by your grace, he daily creates for those like us a creation equal to the duties of the dawn;
and for those born in previous Brahma-kalpas who possess supreme longevity, [he likewise provides].
At that time, emission is like waking from sleep.
O Infinite One, fifty years ago he assumed the form of one half his own age, and indeed he now exists having transcended a *parārdha*;
therein, O Lord, I shall describe those events produced during the final night.
And later, at the arrival of day, [I shall describe] your amorous sports.
Then, at the close of day, the lotus-born Brahmā, desiring deep sleep, dissolved into you;
and the worlds entered your belly, so that this entire universe became a single ocean.
While the world remained as a mere residue of water upon Śeṣa, the king of serpents, who was clad in your very form,
you remained as the embodiment of the experience of intense bliss, your self sealed by the sleep of your own yoga.
In the beginning, you indeed commanded that the power called Kālā be awakened at the conclusion of the dissolution,
while you yourself remained fast asleep there in the abode of all living beings, along with the entire multitude of powers in a state of deep slumber.
O Lord of the Universe, while you, the non-dual one, were thus asleep for a thousand cycles of the four yugas,
the power known as Time, awakened first, indeed roused you from your sleep.
And having awakened, O You who recline within the womb of the waters, you beheld all the worlds dissolved;
then, as those universes remained within yourself in their subtle form, you cast your gaze upon them.

Then, O Beloved! from the cavity of your navel, there arose a certain divine lotus, which was a condensed form containing the entire garland of all objects dissolved within it, appearing as a closing bud.
This very bud of yours, having emerged from your body and grown upon the surface of the water,
has dispelled the impurity of darkness with its rays flashing forth on all sides.
Upon that lotus, held by your power, which was exceedingly variegated with fully blossomed petals,
the lotus-born Brahmā appeared, he whose entire mass of Vedas was self-manifested.
O Supreme Self! Indeed, in this Pādma-kalpa, you have thus raised up the Lotus-born Brahmā; O Viṣṇu, dweller in the ocean, infinite in majesty, destroy the mass of my diseases!
That lotus-born one was indeed situated within the lotus of your navel;
not seeing how this [universe] could have arisen from the ocean,
he turned his face in every direction out of curiosity to behold it.
She assumed four faces, with eight blossoming lotus-eyes.
Beholding only that lotus tossing in the great ocean and taking refuge in it, yet not seeing your body,
who indeed is this one within the vast interior of the lotus? For I am truly helpless.
"From where indeed has this lotus arisen?"—such was the thought that occurred to him.
Having reached the firm conclusion that there must indeed be some cause for that lotus,
that man of mature intellect descended through the hollow of the stalk by means of the science of the power of yoga.
I have seen your most enchanting mind, but not your physical body.
Then, searching through the path of the openings of all the tubes for a hundred years, he saw nothing at all;
returning and sitting comfortably within the heart of a lotus, his mind became one-pointed.
I shall exert the power of concentration, being single-mindedly intent on favoring you.
Indeed, after a hundred years, having been illuminated by the awakening that shines forth from the firm bond of meditative absorption,
that lotus-born one beheld with his inner vision your truly wondrous form, never seen before.
With a deeply satisfied mind, he gazed upon that which rested upon the coils of the serpent's body.
Adorned with a crown, shimmering bracelets, necklaces, and a pair of armlets;
radiant with gems upon his girdle and his yellow garment well-draped around him;
possessing the luster of the *kalāya* flower and the *kaustubha* gem shining upon his chest.
O giver of that very form! I meditate upon [the body] as it was shown to the lotus-born Brahmā.
O Lord of Śrī, O Hari, whose abundant glory is revealed by the various branches of the Vedas! Victory, victory to You, O Master! By good fortune, You have come within the range of my sight;
now quickly grant me an intellect capable of performing the work of creating the universe.
Thus, you whose own greatness of qualities was described by Druhiṇa, protect me!
"O Brahmā, attain unimpaired skill in the creation of the three worlds;
accept my favor and perform further austerities. May there arise in you an exceedingly intense devotion toward me, which accomplishes all goals."
Having uttered these words, he inspired the Creator, whose mind was filled with joy.
Then, having performed austerities for a hundred divine years, he indeed attained the power of asceticism and the power of intellect even greater than before;
and it is said that he beheld a lotus trembling upon the water due to the wind.
Manifesting his power, he drank up both the wind and the waters.
Once again, by your very grace, having fashioned the three worlds with that same lotus, he proceeded to the creation of living beings;
such is the weight of your compassion, O Lord of the Great City in the Realm of the Winds!
Protect me quickly with glances drenched in great compassion.
O Vaikuṇṭha! Having had his strength increased by your grace,
the lotus-born Brahmā indeed created living bodies,
as well as stationary objects consisting of trees and the bodies of animals.
The various castes, the multitudes of human beings, and also the different classes of gods.
Having created these fivefold functions of ignorance— namely, false attachment, the notion of "I," passion, agitation, and fear— he,
being distressed by the production of unrestrained objects of darkness, [proceeded].
Therefore, the remembrance of your feet leads to purification.
Then he created by means of his mind Sanaka, Sananda,
Sanātana, and the sage Sanatkumāra;
they were appointed by him to the task of creation.
Those who relish devotion to your feet did not accept [any other] speech.
While he was thus restraining his rising fury, Śiva, a portion of Bhava, was born from the space between his eyebrows;
"O Viriñci, give me names and steps! he cried out in distress.
Because he wept at that time, he is indeed known by the name Rudra.
Having fashioned Rudra in eleven distinct forms and having bestowed upon him beloved wives and consorts, he, impelled by you,
granted him as many steps.
And he spoke to him, together with his wife, for the purpose of creating progeny.
With the three worlds filled by hosts of Rudras of terrifying form dispatched by Rudra, your mind is stricken with fear;
do not create progeny, but perform austerity for the sake of auspiciousness.
The lotus-born Brahmā, his soul stirred by your words, made a request to him.
Then, from him who was intent on creation, Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Kratu, Pulaha, Pulastya,
Bhṛgu— who was born from his limbs— and Vasiṣṭha and Dakṣa were produced.
And the venerable Śrī Nārada is a servant at your feet.
Then, having created the principles beginning with *dharma* and having produced Kardama and Vāṇī, the Creator became overwhelmed by his offspring;
yet he was awakened by your sons, headed by Sanaka and Dakṣa.
And having been awakened, he ceased, casting off the darkness.
Having brought forth from the multitude of his own mouths all the gods and even the ancient assemblies of all the sciences,
that four-faced one entrusted the increase of creation to those sons.
Not attaining your lotus feet, he became one who took refuge in them.
Then, though unborn, you, knowing the means, divided your body and assumed the states of male and female with Manu and his wife;
and through them, you caused the human races to increase.
O Govinda! O Lord of the City of Marut! Repel all diseases!
O Lord of the abode of Māruta! As creation gradually increased, those divine ones, Sanaka and the others, once approached the world of Vaikuṇṭha in order to behold you.
The lords of sages, having transcended all stages, reached that incomparable abode of yours, which is adorned with delightful groves such as Śreyasa, and with many ponds and jeweled palaces.
O Infinite One, Jaya and Vijaya, the two gatekeepers, blocked those who desired to see you and wished to enter your abode;
yet, O All-pervading Lord, it was solely by your prompting that anger took hold in their hearts.
"Since your conduct is unbecoming of the realm of Vaikuṇṭha, you two shall suffer and take the path of the Daityas!
Thus cursed, those two, who took refuge in Bhava, bowed to them, saying, "May we have the remembrance of Hari."
O lotus-eyed one, having understood this, you have appeared here together with Lakṣmī;
with your beautiful arms resting upon the shoulders of the Lord of Birds, you delight us with your most enchanting form.
Then, having propitiated the lords of sages who were praising you with hymns, those two attendants, finding no other protector, spoke to you with compassion, saying:
"I have approached Bhava through the application of intense passion; please show mercy to me."
Indeed, those two sons of Diti, the heroic enemies of the gods, were born from Kaśyapa as your servants;
they were twins whose efforts were devoted to the arduous task of creating the twilight, and who were like Yama and the Wind to the world.
In former times, there were two brothers known as Hiraṇyakaśipu and Hiraṇyākṣa;
blinded by their own latent impressions, they both obstructed you, their protector, and the entire world with their wrath.
Of those two, the great lord of asuras, Hiraṇyākṣa—his enemy not yet encountered—rushed toward battle;
having submerged the earth, your beloved, into the waters, he roamed about, mace in hand, roaring out of pride.
Then, having heard that you were equal to the Lord of Waters, he wandered about searching for you;
O treasure-house of compassion, you who are visible only to your devotees, O Lord of the abode of the Maruts, restrain my diseases!
Then Svāyambhuva Manu, whose nature is to create living beings,
seeing the earth submerged in water at an improper time,
sought refuge with the Creator through service to Your feet.
In the realm of truth (satyaloka), together with the sages, his intention was one of contentment.
"Alas! The subjects are being created while I am submerged in the earth;
O Lotus-born One, provide a dwelling place for those subjects!"—thus was the Self-existent One addressed by Manu.
O you with eyes like the thighs of a plantain tree, he meditated upon the pair of your feet.
"Alas, alas, O All-pervading Lord! Previously I drank up the waters;
even now the earth is still submerged—what can I do? Thus, I have come for refuge to this pair of Your feet."
From his nostril, he emerged in the form of a young crocodile.
Having first arisen before us with a body the size of a thumb, you then yawned forth with a form like a water-jar;
seeing you thus towering high in the sky, we were struck with wonder.
The Creator, along with his own sons, was struck with amazement.

"Who is this being of inconceivable majesty that has arisen from the cavity of my nostril? Could it be the illusory power (māyā) of the Unconquered One? Thus did the Creator reflect as he became as large as a mountain.
Having come into being instantly, you indeed roared with a most terrible roar.
Hearing that sound of yours, the sages dwelling in Janasthāna and Tapasthāna, who abide in truth, praised you;
with a mind delighted by that hymn of praise, you roared once more.
You, whose form is vast, descended into the reservoir of water.
With his body bristling with hair that rose upward and was smoky-grey, his tail tossed aloft, his terrible snout turned downward,
he swiftly tore through the clouds with his rolling eyes.
O Sage, you have come down, cooling those who praise you.
Then, having entered the waters— filled with swarms of crocodiles, teeming with schools of *timiṅgila* fish, and garlanded with turbid waves—
he, standing in the subterranean realm (*rasātala*), with a terrifying roar, [pierced]...
You did not shake the earth as you searched for him.
O Lord! Having seen you, the deceptive monkey, suddenly cast down into the depths of the netherworld by that wretched Daitya,
you disregarded the attacking charioteers of the enemies of the gods.
With the tip of your fang, you playfully supported the earth.
Then, lifting up the earth, his body appearing even more massive as if marked by the sprouts of *musta* grass caught upon the tips of his tusks,
he rose from the ocean whose fierce waters were surging upward.
O Lord in the form of Kṛtīḍā-Varāha, protect me from disease!
O Giver of Boons! While Hiraṇyākṣa was wandering about, intent on searching for you within the waters of the Saṃvarta deluge that were measured only by his own thighs,
the sage Nārada— whose mind is clever in deceit— went and was devoured by him.
Nandana spoke softly, even while censuring the Danuja, regarding your strength.
"O Lord, that illusory Viṣṇu is seizing your earth! Alas, alas! What is this? Thus addressed by him, the roaring [king] cried out, "Where is he? Where is he? and was shown the path by the sage.
He encountered you, the upholder of the earth, as you were rising from the water.
O Blessed One, disregarding the son of Diti who was laughing, "Aha! This is a wild forest deer," and piercing him with many harsh words,
you looked upon the earth— terrified by his own splendor— with tusks protruding from your head.
Having placed it upon the ocean, you forcefully employed it for the act of crushing adversaries.
While the Daitya held a mace in his hand, you too, grasping a raised mace,
sported with him in hand-to-hand combat amidst a sky resounding with the clashing of maces;
then, as the assembly of gods gathered swiftly out of eagerness to witness the battle, [you struck] him.
"You should restrain yourself before the first twilight," so was it commanded to you by the Creator.
O Lord! When that mace of yours, belonging to the son of Diti, suddenly fell to the ground from the impact of your own mace, alas!
you, whose face was softly smiling, [beheld] that which is skilled at uprooting the race of Danujas.
Having remembered the great wheel and placing it upon the palm of his hand, he desired to shine forth.
Then, as the Daitya, enraged like Time itself, was hurling his trident at you, you severed it by striking with the discus held in your hand; thereupon,
he became violently incensed and struck you with his fist, while you struck him back with equal fury.
O Galanmāyā, indeed all delusions that cause the enchantment of the world reside in you.

Then, when the wheel of illusion had been dispelled by the falling of even a tiny fragment of the light from the wheel of your being, [the Lord] struck that Asura— whose mind was blinded by dense and widespread rage—
with the most heavy blows of his fists.
With the tip of his own hand, he [touched] the base of the ear-hole without limit.
This great-bodied one, crushed by your lotus-hand,
fell with blood streaming from his mouth, while his slaughter was praised by the seers;
at that time, your heart shone with an abundance of unrestrained joy.
The lords of sages praised the body of the sacrifice with dense hymns of praise.

The Vedic meters are in your skin, the bundle of *kuśa* grass in your hair, clarified butter in your eye, the four officiating priests (*caturhotṛ*) in your feet, the sacrificial ladle (*sruk*) in your mouth, the *iḍā* oblation in your belly,
the ritual cups (*graha*) on your tongue, and the chalices (*camasa*) in your ears, O Supreme Person!
O All-pervading One, O Giver of Boons! Soma is the virility, and Upasanda is also in the region of the throat.
O Madhuripu! With a mind gladdened by the praises of the lords of sages, whose mouths were resonant with hymns such as "O Munīndra," and shining with a most exalted form and exceedingly pure fame,
you have reached your own abode, sporting in the essence of bliss.
O Lord of the Abode of Vāyu, may you suppress every single disease of mine!
Constantly recollecting the pair of your feet, that Manu, born from the body of the Lotus-born Brahmā,
spent his time in happiness as he recounted your own conduct, free from all obstacles, within his own heart.
At that time, there indeed lived one named Kardama, born from the shadow of Brahmā;
by his word, he served you, O Blessed One, for ten thousand years with a naturally delightful essence of ghee-offerings.
O Lord! You manifested that body for Kardama, which was as dark as a rain-cloud atop Garuḍa, with lotus-hands shimmering with a playful lotus, and a face radiant with a smile.

To him who was praising you, his body covered with horripilation, you granted your beloved daughter Manu’s daughter, as well as nine other daughters, and your own son Kapila; and having subsequently bestowed upon him your own state, you departed.
That Manu, accompanied by his queen Śatarūpā and their virtuous daughter Devahūtī,
was directed by Nārada as you had instructed and went to Kardama, who was waiting for their arrival.
Having obtained Devahūti, that jewel among young women, who had been offered by Manu, Kardama—
though already satisfied by the worship of Bhava— bestowed his grace upon her through her steadfast service.
Furthermore, by the power of his worship of you, Navātman traveled through the celestial paths with Devahūtī in a celestial chariot created for the sake of his beloved, crowded with throngs of women.

Then, after a hundred years had passed, having obtained nine maidens of auspicious form, he— though intent on departing for the forest— remained, acting for the welfare of his beloveds and eager for the birth of your progeny.
Then, O Lord, when Devahūtī was devoted to serving you at the word of her own husband,
you were born as Kapila, intending to propagate among people the knowledge of the reality of the Supreme Self.
O Kapila! O Madireśa! While Kardama has gone to the forest and my mother is teaching me everything she knows, protect me swiftly from the flood of diseases.

In this world, the intellect attached to the qualities (guṇas) causes bondage, while the intellect unattached to them bestows immortality; yet it is the yoga of devotion that restrains such attachment.
Devotion alone, attainable through following the Great One, is what must be accomplished here.
"You declared to Devahūti that you were 'Kapilatanu' (the one with the body of Kapila)."
Nature, the Great One (Mahat), the Ego (Ahaṅkāra), the subtle elements (Mātrās), the gross elements (Bhūtas), the mind (Hṛt), the ten faculties, and the Puruṣa as the twenty-fifth—
having thus understood their distinctions, one is liberated from Nature.
"You declared to Devahūti that you were Kapilatanu."
This Puruṣa is not stained by the multitude of qualities inherent in Prakṛti; however, if he becomes attached to her, those qualities would affect him.
But through the contemplation of reality and devotion to Me, even she shall depart.
"You declared yourself to Devahūti as 'Kapilatanu' (the one with the body of Kapila)."
One of pure intellect should constantly meditate upon my own form,
seated upon Garuḍa, adorned with divine ornaments and weapons,
and possessing a luster that surpasses the tamāla tree, while being provided with seats and other offerings.
"You declared to Devahūtī that you possess a body of Kapila."
Through hearing of my qualities, virtues, and divine play, and through the currents of my fame, the mind’s inclination toward me becomes like the flood of the celestial river;
that indeed is supreme devotion, for it is the conqueror of death.
"You declared to Devahūtī that you possess a body of golden hue."
Alas! He who, having accumulated wealth through excessive violence, daily nourishes his family, is conquered by women, dotes on children,
and is devoted to the household, enters into torment for being averse to me.
"You spoke thus to Devahūtī: 'Your body shall be of the color of Kapila.'"
Exhausted by the wombs of young women, even one who has attained awakening finds that awakening suddenly slipping away at birth; having overcome childhood through great suffering,
alas, he becomes deluded once again during the time of youth.
"You declared yourself to Devahūti as 'Kapilatanu' (the one with the body of Kapila)."
That righteous householder who performs sacrifices for the hosts of ancestors and gods,
he too falls in due time, traveling upon the southern path;
yet I have performed a deed without desire for the sake of the northern path.
"You spoke thus to Devahūti: 'Your body shall be Kapila.'"
Thus, O Lord, having favored Devahūtī with praise from her whose objects of knowledge were well-known, You departed with the hosts of yogis;
then she, possessed of stainless intellect, was liberated through the yoga of devotion.
You also abide as a sacred ford for the welfare of people in the north-eastern direction.

O Supreme One! What need is there for much speaking? You indeed declare that devotion to your lotus feet removes all fears and bestows all desires; having cast away my ailments, may you [grant them] to me.
O Lord of Gurupavanapura! Bestow devotion upon me.
Then Daśa, the son of Viriñca, having obtained Prasūti as his wife, begot here sixteen daughters;
he gave thirteen to Dharma and Svadhā to the Pitṛs.
To Giriśa, who is a portion of you, and to Svāhā, the virtuous wife who consumes the oblation.
For Mūrti, the wife of Dharma, gave birth to you, Nārāyaṇa, who is a friend to men and possesses exalted majesty—
at whose birth the gods were delighted and raised the cry of victory.
The hosts of gods rained down heaps of flowers and offered hymns of praise.

The Daitya possesses a thousand armors, surrounded by defenses obtained through austerities and battles lasting a thousand years; you two have likewise fashioned your austerities and battles in successive turns.
They struck down this [enemy], who had only one suit of armor remaining, along with his elephant.
Even while practicing and teaching the dharma of liberation,
you dwelt in the midst of Badarikāśrama together with your brothers;
then Śakra, his soul rendered powerless by your tranquility and the power of your asceticism, [approached].
He sent forth Māra, who was surrounded by celestial women.
Desire, acting as an ally to the spring and the Malaya breeze,
repeatedly pierces me with the arrows of his beloved’s side-long glances— arrows bristling with blossoming charms— and beholding you, he remains unshaken.
Then, filled with fear, he addressed you with a gentle smile.
"O celestial nymphs, enough of this fear! Dwell here in my heart," so saying,
you were addressed by those who stood all around in wonder, offering their praise.
You displayed those women whose eyes were timid with fear, even as they served you.
Madana and the others, who had assembled for the purpose of deluding [the world], were indeed rendered senseless by the fragrances of your maidservants;
and all that was offered by you, they accepted out of sheer shame.
Her, Urvaśī, who humbles the pride of the inhabitants of heaven.
Having seen Urvaśī and heard the story, Śakra became agitated upon realizing your greatness; thus,
this incarnation is exceedingly peaceful and beautiful.
O granter of boons, there is none superior to you; you alone are the very body of Kṛṣṇa.
But Dakṣa, blinded by passion through excessive indulgence, was not very respectful toward you, and thus there arose a painful agitation;
because of that, he obstructed even your own body, O Śarva.
And Yajña married his own daughter to Vairapiśuna.
But he, whose sacrifice was crushed by the enraged Śiva, had his head severed; then,
having been restored to life by Hara through the grace of the gods,
and having completed his excellent sacrifice with your assistance, he regained peace once more.
O you who bring about peace, O Lord of the City of the Maruts, protect us!
Suruci was the wife of King Uttānapāda, the son of Manu, and she was exceedingly beloved by him;
the other, named Sunīti, was not so favored by her husband.
Having no other recourse, she has eternally come to you alone for refuge.
Seeing that excellent son of Suruci on his father’s lap, Dhruva— the son of Sunīti— was indeed about to climb up; at that,
the child was reportedly addressed quite harshly by Suruci.
Indeed, envy arises from those who are free from the cycle of existence.
While your father, deluded by you, looked on helplessly at his wife,
he was struck down by harsh words and went far away to his own mother;
she too, for the sake of crossing over the course of her own karma among men—
He pointed out your very feet as the refuge for the child.
Having heard this, that proud youth, having resolved his mind upon your worship, departed from the city at the age of five;
he was one who had clearly perceived the path of mantras revealed by Nārada.
I propitiated you with ascetic penance at the edge of the Madhuka forest.
When his father had returned to the city with a despondent heart, his state of mind was consoled by the venerable Nārada; meanwhile,
the boy’s mind remained fixed upon you, as he grew up step by step.
Indeed, by means of rigorous austerity, he spent five months.
At that time, when the horizons were rendered breathless by the power of asceticism, you, whose heart was moistened with compassion at the request of the gods,
appeared before him whose mind was dissolved in the nectar of the consciousness of your form.
O All-pervading Lord, you have manifested yourself, mounted upon Garuḍa!
Perceiving him— whose heart was rippling with the intense joy of beholding you,
as if submerged in the aesthetic savor of your form— with his two eyes, and desiring to offer praise, [he touched] the region of his cheek.
You have touched it with both fear and such great reverence.
Having understood his state of mind, you should address that deer, whose purity is awakened by wisdom,
saying: "After enjoying sovereignty for a long time, you shall again resort to [the life of a sage]."
The supreme, eternal state, free from cessation.
When you had spoken thus and departed, that prince,
who gladdened all people, returned to the city and rejoiced for a long time, his desires fulfilled by your grace.
And when my father had gone to the forest, I was unable to bear the burden of the kingdom.
O King! When this supreme [city] had been struck down by the yakṣas, he, intent on battle with the yakṣas, desisted from the words of Manu;
for he had obtained peace from the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada), whose heart was now gracious.
The Great-Souled One chose only your devotion, which was exceedingly firm.
Having previously traveled by the celestial chariot brought by your attendants,
he now dwells joyfully at the station of Dhruva together with his mother;
thus, you are one whose mind is intent on protecting your own servants.
O Lord of the Abode of Wind! Restrain the floods of my diseases!
To that Tuṅgakīrti, born of the Dhruva lineage, was born a son named Vena;
his mind, pained by the faults of that excellent king—
With his mind fixed upon your feet, he departed for the forest.
Even the wicked Vena, though of feeble prowess, was installed by the citizens and others for the protection of the earth,
while he himself praised only his own strength above all else.
This man has obstructed your sacrifices upon the circle of the earth.
When he arrived at the hermitage to offer beneficial counsel,
those lords of sages, thinking "there is no other householder besides me," became intent on speaking words of reproach against you.
Vena was reduced to the state of a moth in the fire of the curse.
When that [sin] was destroyed, the lords of sages— who are fearful of base people— abandoned it from their own limbs, which had been long protected by those very [sins],
once the sin had been removed from that thoroughly crushed and formidable pillar of a thigh.
When the staff-like arms were being crushed, you manifested yourself.
Renowned as Pṛthu, his future immense prowess praised by bards and others instructed by ascetics,
he [saw] the earth whose prosperity had been swallowed up by the distress of Vena.
He made her, who had been seized by his own bow, equal to himself.
Furthermore, in appropriate and beautiful vessels, the gods and others, together with the dear ones who are the leaders of their own families,
[offered] whatever desired foods and such things there were.
At your will, you have milked from your fragrant body [the essence].
O Lord of the Three Abodes,
when you had commenced the hundredth horse sacrifice, Indra,
the performer of a hundred sacrifices, being full of rivalry, approached you in humble guise along with his friends.
Having stolen your son's horse, he was defeated.

When the Lotus-born Lord, at the conclusion of the sacrifice, sought to restrain the King of the Gods as he repeatedly attempted to cast that steed into the fire within the circle of the foremost sages;
You yourself directly beheld Madhuripu as his very self.
O Lord! Having obtained that boon, having established my sole devotion at the edge of the Gaṅgā,
may you at some time proclaim blessings to the multitude of sages residing here.
You did not behold the sages headed by Sanaka standing before you.
Maintaining that consciousness which was uttered from the mouths of Sanaka and the others,
he himself became a dweller in the forest depths;
O Lord of such a vast form, [be] quickly [gracious] to me!
O dweller in the abode of wind, pacify the flood of diseases!
Pṛthudharmakarmaṭha, the grandson of Pṛthu, begot upon his two young wives, Śatadrū and Īḍā,
sons named Pracetas who were possessed of noble minds, as if they were the sprouts of your compassion.
By the command of their father, who was intent on the desire to create, all ten of them became devoted to asceticism;
having gone to the western ocean, they beheld a charming lake upon its shore.
Then Bhava, having arrived at this sacred ford of yours, honored by the sight of your devotees,
appeared before the lords of the waters (the Vasus) and taught them this hymn of praise to you, the supreme devotee.
Chanting your hymn of praise within the waters, these beings have served you for ten thousand years;
yet, due to their relish for the taste of your bliss, even this kalpa has passed for them as swiftly as a moment, like the fixed movement of the pole star.
Purified by their excessively increasing austerities, even he who was devoted to the violence of sacrifice became purified;
and their father as well, having had the Self revealed to him by Nārada through the discipline of the householder, attained the state of being the Self.
Then, by the power of their compassion, you appeared before the Pracetasas, mounted upon the king of birds,
with eight arms whose splendor was uplifted by the rays of your radiant discus and other excellent weapons.
To the sons of Pracetas, even as they were entreating you, you yourself granted the waters out of an abundance of compassion;
may this reflection upon you also lead to the welfare of embodied beings, and may this hymn to Rudra grant all desires.
"Having obtained my daughter, the beloved of the trees, enjoy yourself with her for ten hundred thousand years;
let there be a capable son, and indeed, at that very moment, you shall depart from me"—thus he spoke to them with sheer joy.
Then, as they were angrily burning the trees that covered the surface of the earth, they were restrained by Brahmā;
and having obtained that daughter given by the trees, they lived happily for the duration of time you specified.

Having obtained Dakṣa as their son and performed the sacrifice, the Pracetasas attained the state of bliss through the wisdom received from Nārada; O Lord, O Master of Vātālaya, may You likewise bestow that upon me—protect me!
For Nābhi was born from King Āgnīdhra, who was as dear a son to Priyavrata as a son could be;
having seen you, the bestower of desired things, in the midst of those who seek their desires, he has performed the sacrificial rites solely for your satisfaction.

O You of Universal Form! Having been praised there by the lords of sages while the king was requesting a son equal to Yourself, You vanished from the sacrificial ground, saying, "I shall be born myself."
Then, through a portion of yourself, you were born as the one named Ṛṣabha in the womb of Merudevī, the beloved of Nābhi;
by the power of your extraordinary qualities and majesty, you brought joy to all people without exception.

Having entrusted the burden of sovereignty to you, the sustainer of the three worlds, Nābhi, together with Merudevī, reached the forest of asceticism; serving you, he has indeed gone to that state of yours which is the abode of bliss.
When Indra, out of indignation caused by your superior excellence, did not send rain upon this land of Ajana,
you then, through the power of your own yoga, made this very land well-rain-favored.
Then, although his heart was devoted to the Self, he married Jayantī, the lovely daughter of Indradatta whom he had won;
and there he begot a hundred sons, of whom King Bharata was the firstborn.
Nine other excellent yogis became new [rulers], while nine others protected the regions of Bhāratavarṣa;
those eighty-one remaining sons of yours attained the status of Brahmins through the power of their asceticism.
Having thus taught the path of liberation characterized by detachment and devotion to his sons in the midst of the lords of sages,
he himself adopted the conduct of a paramahaṃsa and subsequently assumed the behavior of one who is dull-witted, insane, or a ghost.

Though he had become the Supreme Self, he moved throughout the entire earth, free from all change, absorbed in the essence of the Self which is devoid of diminution, even as he gave instruction to others and was disregarded by everyone.

O Lord of the Wind! Having long practiced the vow of the dog, the conduct of the cow, the deer, and the crow, and having attained Your supreme essential nature, You whose body was carried away by fire on Mount Kuṭaka—dispel my sufferings!
In the central region of the earth known as Ilāvṛta,
where the female population consists solely of women preeminent in beauty,
he was being properly worshipped by Śarva with mantras and hymns of praise.
O Supreme Lord, whose essence is Saṅkarṣaṇa, I take refuge in you.
In the eastern region of Ilāvṛta, known as Bhadrāśva,
[he was] being praised by the sages called Bhadraśravas;
he is expert in extracting the Vedas hidden at the end of the kalpa.
I meditate, O Lord, upon you in the form of Hayashirsha.
I meditate upon Him who resides in the southern region of Harivarṣa, attended by eminent beings headed by Prahlāda,
possessing a lofty, peaceful, and pure white form— He who is uniquely pure.
O Blessed One! You are Narahari, the bestower of knowledge.
In the western continent of Ketumāla,
which is playful in nature, he dwells with limbs beautified by smiles of exquisite grace,
attended by Lakṣmī and the sons of Prajāpati.
I worship you, who have assumed a body of desire for the sake of her beloved.
In the delightful region named Uttara-Ramya to the north, he indeed shines— worshipped with royal ceremonies by the lord of that land,
and appearing among those whose hearts are free from envy and who are singularly devoted to him.
O Lord of the World, I worship you in the form of a fish.
Aryaman, the foremost of the host of Pitṛs, dwells in the year known as Hiraṇmaya, seated in the northern region, whose body is the hermitage dedicated to the task of supporting the mountains.
I worship you, O Blessed One! O Self consisting of pure consciousness!
Moreover, in the northern continent of Uttarakuru, he was served by the beloved Dharaṇī with various kinds of honored mantras and praises;
his most majestic body had its broad back rubbed by the tips of her tusks.
Protect me, O you who possess the form of the wise and noble sacrificial boar!
In the southern direction, in the region known as Kiṃpuruṣa,
he dwells, attended by Hanumān who possesses firm devotion;
he is endowed with a most wonderful form that delights Sītā.
O Viṣṇu, shining forth as the very soul of Rāma, protect me completely!
Together with Śrī Nārada and the foremost leaders of Bhāratakhaṇḍa, being worshipped through the praises of Sāṅkhya and Yoga,
may you protect the virtuous here until the end of the kalpa.
O Nārāyaṇa, friend of men, O Infinite One, protect me!
In Plakṣa they worship the form of the Sun; in Śālmala, the form of the Moon; in the continent named Kuśa, the form of Fire;
in Krauñca, the form of Water; and in Śāka, the form of Wind.
O Mother, in the world named Puṣkara, people [worship] you in the form of Brahman.
With all the constellations beginning with Dhruva, the clusters of stars, and the planets being assigned to your various limbs starting from the tail,
you are worshipped by the great ones in the form of a porpoise.
O you who lie upon the ocean, block hell for me during the twilights!
In the region at the base of Pātāla, I behold you in the form of Śeṣa, with a thousand heads resplendent with a single swinging earring,
clad in blue garments, holding a plow, and surrounded by the wives of the serpents.
O Lord of the Guru’s house, I worship you, who are beloved, so that you may remove my afflictions.

O Lord! In former times, a householder named Ajāmila, while treading the path of dharma, went to the forest at the word of his guru and saw there a woman of loose character, intoxicated with passion, though she appeared to possess excellent conduct.

Although he was by nature tranquil, his mind was drawn away by her; abandoning his own duty and engaging with her, he became a perpetrator of unrighteousness. Having reached the tenth stage of life, he nevertheless placed his affection upon a son born of her, who was joined with worldly existence.
At the time of death, perceiving the three terrifying messengers of King Yama and trembling with fear,
he previously invoked by the power of even a slight latent impression of mindfulness of you the son named Nārāyaṇa.
Even for one of wicked intent, by the mere power of even a single syllable of Your name uttered at that moment,
Your enchanting four-armed attendants, clad in yellow garments, rushed forward from before him.
And as the soldiers were dragging him away after seizing him, these people forcibly rushed forward, crying out, "Release him!
They were then restrained by the attendants of the Lord, who informed them of all that man's wickedness.
"O wise ones, how can there be punishment even when an expiation has been performed?
Is no expiation known to those like you?"—thus did your men speak, O Lord!
"O Lord! Your devotees have declared that while vows and other practices enjoined by the Śruti and Smṛti purify sin, they do not cut away latent impressions (vāsanā);
however, service to the Infinite cuts away both."

"O Lord! By this, even for sins committed over thousands of millions of births, atonement has been made. "He has taken the name of Hari," they said, O Master, as your men spoke while agitated by fear.

O Lord! Your servants have declared that even for men who chant the praises of Mukunda without conscious intent, it burns away the masses of their sins; such is its majesty, just as fire consumes fuel and medicine cures diseases.
When the messengers of Yama had departed upon these words and the host of your own soldiers had vanished,
that man— practicing mindfulness of you for some time— attained your state through the very soldiers of yours.

O Lord, O Sovereign of the Wind’s Abode, protect me! Fearing that his own servants might report [the matter], Yama strictly instructed his subordinates: "Do not go among those who are devoted to your feet!"
Furthermore, O Blessed One, another Dakṣa named Pracetas also performed service to you, desiring the expansion of creation;
at that time, you manifested with eight resplendent arms.
He granted him a boon and gave him that dark-complexioned bride.
O Lord, ten thousand of his sons, and again a thousand,
attained your path through the word of the illustrious Nārada;
he did not release the curse upon the sage because they did not dwell together in one place.
But the supreme devotee Ṛṣi Anugraha regarded me alone as such.
Then, from his sixty daughters, Viśvarūpa produced floods of progeny; subsequently, that son of his daughter became his grandson,
who caused Indra— armored by your hymn of praise— to be defeated in battle.
O Lord! Your majesty is indeed all-conquering.
Formerly, it is said, in the realm of Śūrasena, there was a king named Citraketu who, through the power of Aṅgiras, obtained an only son.
Then, when his co-wife’s son was killed there—
He was deluded by your illusion and became helpless against the hosts.
Then the compassionate Nārada, together with Aṅgiras, arrived there and, having revealed the life of the son,
dispelled his delusion through the words, "Whose son am I?"
Having abandoned [other duties], he appointed the king to the ritual of worshipping you.
Having then received from Nārada both a hymn and a mantra for the propitiation of your Śeṣa-form, he indeed performed austerities;
for at the end of seven nights, he attained the sovereignty of the Vidyādharas.
Having attained this exceedingly dull intellect, he devoted himself to you.

To him, appearing soon thereafter, the Lord became gracious through hymns of praise, manifesting in a form as white as a lotus stalk with a thousand heads, surrounded by hosts of Siddhas who had offered their adoration.
Having bestowed the reality of the Self and having shown favor, you have vanished.
Then he too, the crest-jewel of your devotees, with a joyful mind, for a hundred thousand times ten million years, will wander at will through the worlds,
singing of your multitude of virtues along with beautiful women.
Devoid of any company, he moved about gracefully.
Driven by you, he has surely gone to the Silver Mountain (Rūpyagiri) in order to dissolve his excessive attachment; there, in a great assembly,
he sits without fear upon the lap of the enemy of Aṅga’s son (Kārttikeya), who holds his beloved in his embrace.
Mocking that Śaṅkara, Umā addressed him.
Free from agitation, having obtained release from the curse without being asked,
he became the asura Vṛtra and fought the lord of the gods;
through his devotion and his explanations of the reality of the self, he performed wonders in battle.
Having dispelled even the enemy's delusion, he has gone to your state.
By serving you, Diti, though intent on slaying Indra, instead obtained those Maruts who are friends of Indra; thus,
service to you bestows auspicious results even upon one of wicked intent.
O Lord of the Wind-dweller, protect me, for you are such a one!
O Lord, when Hiraṇyākṣa was slain by you in the form of the preeminent Boar, his innate resolve— exhausted by his habitual anger—
was reduced to a mere beginning for gold in the assembly of the enemies of the gods.
O Enemy of Mura, it is said that for the sake of your own destruction, you have made a mere vow!
Having performed austerities for no long time, he indeed beheld before him the terrible Creator, who is eternal and worshipped by gods, humans, animals, and others;
having obtained a boon, the arrogant one proclaimed here in this world that He was his own leader.
Disregarding you, he seized heaven from Indra while tearing it apart.
To slay you and your enemy who has attained your state,
you concealed yourself within his heart with a subtle form while he looked outward;
yet even there, roaring loudly, you sought him out to the ends of the entire world.
Thinking they had fled out of fear, he, indeed appearing as a victor, turned back.
Then a son named Prahlāda was born to that sage while he was still in the womb; having attained the greatness of devotion to You even while in the womb,
though he was by birth a Daitya, he felt affection for You even as a child.
O Giver of Boons, you have become the supreme example for those devoted to you.
Seeing that the laughter of the enemies of the gods was actually service at your feet,
he— whose soul was guided by destiny— instructed him for a long time through his teachers;
yet he firmly regarded this instruction of the guru as leading to misfortune.
Dispelling all [those obstacles], he grew solely through devotion to your feet.
When his son asked, "What is the best among those subjects studied?
and the boy replied that it was devotion to you, the father, his composure becoming deeply agitated, he grew angry with his teachers; yet his innate intelligence immediately perceived the truth.
In this world of suffering, may [all beings] become those who have taken refuge at your feet.

O Supreme Self, O All-pervading Lord! Alas, though he was pierced by spears, severely crushed by the hosts of world-elephants, bitten by great serpents, deprived of food through fasting, and even cast down from the king of mountains— [he remains steadfast].
Because he had entrusted his very self to you, he did not suffer any affliction whatsoever.
Then, overcome with suspicion, his father— who was exceedingly wicked—
bound him in that house with Varuṇa-nooses at the command of the preceptor;
and in the absence of the preceptor, he [the father] bound the other sons of the Daityas who were his followers.
He also taught the supreme reality and knowledge concerning devotion to you.
Hearing his entire assembly of children intent on praising you, the father, blinded by rage, said to him: "You wretch of a family! What strength do you have?
[The boy replied: "My strength is Vaikuṇṭha; and he is the strength of yours and of the worlds as well."
"This very one is the entire threefold world," thus spoke this wise man.
"Ha! Where is he? Where is that Hari, the soul of the entire world?
Thus did the son of Diti break the pillar, his sword drawn.
Therefore, O Viṣṇu, I am not able to speak [of him] suddenly.
O Compassionate One! O Soul of the Universe! O Dweller in the City of Wind! Have mercy on me!
As Hiraṇyakaśipu struck against the pillar,

your terrible roar arose, pulverizing his ears and filling the hollow of the cosmic egg; indeed, having heard it, the heart of the Daitya king was struck with fear, for such a sound had never been heard by him before.
A certain trembling fell upon him, and even the lotus-born Brahmā was shaken from his world.
While the Daitya cast his eyes in all directions, O Lord, your body—which had arisen from the pillar and was neither of the form of a beast nor of a human—was filled with great fury.
As the Asura’s mind became utterly bewildered, wondering, "What is this? What is this terrifying wonder? [the Lord spoke].
You yawned, your body expanding with the bristling of fierce, white, quivering hair.
May this body of yours be victorious— its eyes rolling and exceedingly harsh like molten gold, its mane and whiskers trembling so violently that they seem to pierce the very sky;
its mouth wide open like a vast cavern, and its great sword leaping fiercely.
Terrifying with a pair of enormous fangs visible as his tongue protrudes.
With a jaw made terrifying by rising folds of skin, a neck short and exceedingly thick, and intensely formidable from afar due to the cruel rays of the nails protruding from hundreds of stout arms;
he was one who, with a deep roar like that of a massive cloud leaping across the sky, caused all beings to flee.
I bow to that Nārasiṃha form of yours, which is a mass of competitive rivalry.
"Surely this one is Viṣṇu; I shall slay him!"—thinking thus, you seized with your two broad arms that lord of the Daityas as he rushed forward, terrifying with his whirling mace.
Then the hero, having escaped, underwent various exertions while grasping sword and shield.
Revealing [himself], he flew up once more toward you, who were intent on devouring the world—oh!
Seizing that lowest of demons as he was wandering once more with both arms,
she swiftly threw him down at the door upon her two thighs; then, tearing out her claws into the region of his chest,
she pierced him so that blood flowed copiously from within his belly, creating a festive spectacle.
Drinking again and again, he let out a lion’s roar that destroys many worlds.
Having swiftly abandoned that slain [demon], while you were leaping up and devouring the entire host of Daityas— your towering body drenched by waves of blood—
the earth began to whirl, the oceans trembled, and the multitude of mountains shook violently.
Alas, the world of moving and non-moving beings, with its birds soaring upward, has fallen into a most wretched state.

No one in this world was able to approach you while you stood in the midst of the assembly with a body terrifying from the flesh and fat you had consumed, wearing a garland of formidable entrails, your fierce wrath ignited, and your heavy, irresistible roar resounding; the cowards remained far away.
All of them, headed by Śarva, Viriñca, and Vāsava, each offered praise individually.
Once again, when the child Prahlāda, rendered fearless, bowed at his feet within the abode of the medicinal herbs (Akṣatauṣadhi) by the command of Brahmā, you, overwhelmed by a burden of compassion,
laid your hand upon his head; then, being pacified, he was uplifted by hymns of praise.
Thus, even though his mind was free from desire, he granted this boon for the sake of favoring the world.
O Lord who thus displays fierce gestures, O Sovereign whose entire majesty is clearly sung in the Upanishads known as the Śrītāpanīya, O You of perfectly pure form—
who indeed could ever transgress You, the one who is supreme over all such [beings]?
O beloved of Prahlāda! O Lord of the City of the Maruts! Protect me from all disease!
Indradyumna, the sovereign of the Pāṇḍya region, whose soul was devoted to you, once on Mount Candana—
his mind immersed in service to you— did not even notice Agastya when he arrived, desiring hospitality.
"O you who were born from a jar, burdened with a weight of accumulated anger and stiffened in soul, become an elephant!
Having thus cursed him, he departed; and he too attained the state of a lordly elephant, blessed by the manifestation of your remembrance.

Sporting on Mount Trikūṭa situated in the midst of the ocean of milk with his female companions, this leader of the herd surpassed all living beings by his power; for where is there no attainment of excellence for those devoted to you?
By virtue of his divine body and power, remaining firm and unaware of fatigue,
he once took delight with his herds in a lake on the edge of a mountain, though exhausted by the heat, being impelled by you.

Hūhū, who had become a crocodile in that water by the curse of Devala, seized this elephant by its hind leg; for you are the remover of fatigue for your own people, acting thus for the sake of pacification.
Due to the power of your service, he fought for a thousand years with irresistible force;
when the time had come for him to achieve one-pointed concentration on your feet, you made that heroic elephant seize him like a crocodile.

With devotion arising from the knowledge of his former state made manifest through distress, and worshipping with ichor sprayed from his trunk, he uttered that most excellent hymn—previously practiced and centered on the non-dual Self—to the Supreme Soul: "O Supreme Soul!"
Having heard this entire hymn centered on the attributeless, which Brahmā, Īśa, and the others could not utter because they thought "I am not [He]," You,
the Soul of All, were seen before them mounted upon Tārkṣya, impelled by the force of Your abundant compassion.
Having seized that lordly elephant with your lotus-like hand, you tore apart the foremost of crocodiles with your discus;
when this Gandharva was released from his curse, that elephant attained a form identical to yours and shone brilliantly.
"Whoever should sing this account concerning you and me at dawn shall attain the highest welfare.
Having said this, you went with him to your abode; O Viṣṇu, Lord of the wind's dwelling, protect us!

Durvāsas, having personally presented a divine garland obtained from the celestial nymphs as an offering to Śakra, saw it crushed there by the elephant of the Lord of Serpents; what forbearance can there be for those born from the portions of deities other than you?
Then, when the lord of the gods was afflicted by a curse that brought manifest old age, and when the gods were defeated by the asuras and shorn of their luster,
Śarva and all the other deities approached the lotus-born Brahmā and together sought refuge in you, O source of liberation.

O Giver of Boons! At that time, Your greatness was praised by Brahmā and the other gods; appearing before them with Your supreme splendor, You commanded: "O Devas! Having made peace with the offspring of Diti, churn the nectar!"
When the host of gods had formed an alliance with the Dānavas and was leading Mount Mandara as a churning-stick in their intoxication,
you, O Lord of Birds, suddenly placed the ocean in the water, carrying it like a jujube fruit while that mountain fell away.
Then, having quickly placed Vāsuki as the rope upon the ocean where all the seeds had been cast,
when the gods and demons began the process of churning, you, under the pretext of that task, placed the enemies of the gods within the mouth of the serpent.
