At that time, when the ocean of milk— with its waters agitated and its depths churned— had sunk down under the weight of a massive burden,
and while the gods were in the greatest distress, you, seeking their welfare and desiring to preserve their lives, assumed the form of a tortoise with a hard shell.
O Viṣṇu, with your body— which was as firm as a diamond, a hundred thousand yojanas in extent,
and which had entered the depths of the ocean— you lifted up the submerged Lord of Mountains.
When the king of mountains had suddenly sunk, they all then rubbed him firmly with joy;
having entered even the pair of serpent-kings, you increased their strength while pacifying their agitation.

O Unswerving One, Brahmā, Śiva, and the other gods, having become utterly bewildered with joy, offered you hymns while raining down flowers, as they held their lotus-hands steady upon the lordly mountains that were being tossed upward by the force of your violent whirling.

O Lord! When the host of Daityas was scorched by the wind from the mouths of serpents, and the race of the gods was likewise somewhat distressed by that very same force, it is said that out of compassion for you, the clouds rained upon the hosts of immortals, but not upon the multitudes of Daityas.
The poison Kālakūṭa, which was like flickering fire, surged forth from the front of the ocean;
then Śiva, overwhelmed with joy at the hymns of praise from the immortals, drank it down for the sake of your beloved.
O Lord of the Three Abodes! While the gods and asuras were contending with one another, Surabhi was born; she bestowed herself threefold upon the sages.
Then the jewel of horses appeared, followed by the jewel of elephants, and the celestial nymphs who cause the gambling among the gods.
O Lord of the World! At that time, the goddess Kamalā became devoted to you and was most beautiful;
beholding her stainless form, the entire world of living beings was filled with longing.
At that very moment, when you had given your heart to the Goddess, the Lord of the Thirty-three presented her with a jeweled pedestal;
then the sages consecrated her with all the materials required for anointment and with the words of the Vedas.
The gods and others adorned her— whose creeper-like limbs were graced by side-glances charming due to their following the water of consecration—
with jeweled earrings, yellow garments, necklaces, and other such ornaments.

Wearing a bridal wreath resonant with the humming of bees, her gait slowed by the weight of her jar-like breasts and the tinkling of her anklets sweetening her steps, she approached you long ago, manifesting both bashfulness and grace.
Having perceived that even all the gods, beginning with Giriśa and Dhruṇin, though partakers of virtue, are never free from even a trace of defect,
she has placed this divine garland upon you alone, who are eternally most delightful.
With your chest, you swiftly measured out this world, the mother of all beings, who is of no other nature;
through the rain of the beauty of those eyes shining from your breast, the entire universe was nourished.
At that time, the intoxicating wine (vāruṇī), which causes extreme delusion and confusion, indeed arrived;
you, however, gave it over to the great asuras with excessive honor, thereby granting it the path of darkness.
Then, beautiful as a fresh rain-cloud, you indeed arose from the ocean as Dhanvantari, bearing the nectar in a vessel with both hands; O Lord of the abode of the Wind, remove all suffering!
O Lord! While the Daityas were snatching the nectar from your rising hand, you consoled the gods who were left without refuge and then vanished;
this was through your own power.
The sons of Diti became like those who had started a quarrel with their own herd.
At that time, you attained a dark-complexioned body, both in luster and age, curved by the high mounds of her breasts;
yet all [the gods], having abandoned their quarrel over the jar of nectar, [honored you].
Agitated by thirst, they hastened toward the jar-like breasts of your chest.
"Who are you, O fawn-eyed one? Distribute this nectar!"—to these [demons] who, helpless with rising passion, were thus entreating her, she replied:
"O Daityas, how can you trust me when I am an unchaste woman?"
Thus she spoke, her eyes full of deep trust and her body bowed low.
As they joyfully presented jars of nectar to these [beings], she,
saying "Forgive my misdeed," assigned the gods and demons their respective places in separate rows.
With playful and graceful movements, they became intoxicated by that nectar.
While those gods stood silent, thinking, "She is devoted to us," you, having finished distributing the nectar among the deities,
assumed your own form, being subject to the will of the world of your devotees.
You struck down Svarbhānu, who had half-drunk the nectar.
When you had departed after giving to others that fruit worthy of being used for the extraction of nectar, the gods indeed seized it from you; then,
as the battle grew fierce, the illusory power of the Daitya Bali began to overwhelm them.
While the hosts of gods were utterly bewildered, you manifested yourself here.

You have slain Kālanemi and Māli along with his followers; Śakra slew Bala, Jambha, and Vala together with their kin; and Namuci was cut down when he had become difficult to kill, whether in his dry or moist state.
With foam and the words of Nārada, he checked that battle.
O Maheśa, having heard that you had assumed a female form to enchant the Danujas, he became curious to behold it;
accompanied by the Bhūtas and Girijā, he went to your abode.
Having praised him, he spoke his desire, and then you vanished from sight.
And at the boundary of the grove, seeing you— lovely and charming, with eyes flickering in the playful sport of striking a ball, and your garment slipping away— this Mind-born One [Kāma]...
O body of the enemy of Ananga, he embraced you with impetuous force!
Once again, having pursued her as she fled, the Lord—
whose supreme realization of ultimate truth blossomed through the emission of his semen—
spoke of your greatness to the Goddess, honoring you.
O Lord whose abode is the wind, may you be such as that!
Although the high-souled Bali was struck down by Śakra in battle, he had his body restored to life by Śukra; his vital heat increased through sacrifices,
he became valorous, and he [rescued] the three worlds where the gods were cowering in fear.
He brought the wheel under his control, remaining fearless even before the face of that wheel.
Overcome with grief upon seeing her sons' suffering, Aditi sought refuge with her husband, Kāśyapa;
for it was he who had previously instructed her in that worship known as the milk-vow (payovrata).
For twelve days, she practiced while being filled with devotion toward you.
When her mind was thus absorbed in you at the appointed time,
you yourself appeared before her in a dark form with four arms; and as she bowed there, you said, "May I become your son."
"You must keep my gaze secret," you said, as you departed.
At that time, while you were established in asceticism under Kāśyapa,
you were impelled by the Creator and entered the womb of Aditi;
and she gave birth to you, who possess a manifest and divine form like that of Viṣṇu.
On that twelfth lunar day, the auspicious day of Śravaṇa, she [approached] you.
While the host of gods, overwhelmed with joy and sounding the music of celestial instruments, rained down showers of flowers upon that holy hermitage,
his body was joined by his parents with palms pressed together, crying out, "Victory! Victory!"
At that moment, you assumed the form of an exceptionally sharp-witted young brahmin.

O Lord of radiant form! Having been brought before the faces of the Lords of Creatures (Prajāpatis) and honored with the girdle of muñja grass, the staff, the deerskin, the rosary of beads, and other such emblems, you have performed the fire-sacrifice (agnikārya).
You set out for the house of Bali, where the horse sacrifice was being performed.
Shaking the earth as if to reveal beforehand the weight appropriate to your future greatness, you departed,
bearing a parasol as if to ward off the heat of others' envy.
And he was able to inflict punishment upon the hosts of Dānavas as if they were right before his eyes.
When you had reached that sacrificial hall for the horse-sacrifice on the northern bank of the Narmadā, people, their eyes dazzled by your radiance, wondered:
"Is this the sun, or fire, or perhaps Sanatkumāra?"
"Who indeed is this yogi? they wondered, with doubt expressed through the mouths of Śuka and the others.
Quickly brought by the Bhṛgus, who were overwhelmed by your majesty,
the virtuous Asura approached you of beautiful form with devotion; his limbs covered in horripilation, he bathed your feet.
Therefore, this is held upon the head as the most sacred of all sacred places.
Whether by virtue of being born in the lineage of Prahlāda, or through his devotion to the twice-born via sacrifices,
even this son of Diti obtained that which is to be cherished upon the head of Śiva— the water from his feet.
Therefore, O All-pervading Lord, abode of the Guru, may you protect me!
With affection, the Daitya, his great body gazing upon you,
spoke while joining his palms in añjali to you, O Unconquered One, as he worshipped you:
"O son of a Brahmin, tell me, what is it that you desire from me?"
I shall give away everything—wealth, food, a house, or even the earth itself.
Having heard those words of Bali, which were inexhaustible, you— though filled with compassion—
desiring to quell his arrogance, praised the lineage of the Daityas and requested from him only as much land as could be measured by three steps.
But when it is said, "Give me everything," who would not be moved to laughter?
"O fool, why do you ask me, the Lord of All, for three paces of land here? Choose the entire earth instead!"—thus he spoke to you with pride;
yet out of that very pride, being unable to fulfill those three paces, he uttered words of insult.
And he, though unworthy of it, underwent bondage for the sake of profound peace.
O Giver of Boons, when it was said, "If you are not delighted by the three worlds, nor satisfied even by the earths," and you were then desirous of giving water,
the preceptor of the Daityas, indeed impelled by one seeking to test you, [offered it] to you.
"Do not give me! This is Hari! he spoke quite clearly.
"If that Blessed One thus entreats me, I shall certainly give it, for my desire is fulfilled"— so saying, even though cursed by Kāvya, the Daitya [offered] to you,
to whom Vindhyāvalī, his own beloved wife, had offered water for the feet.
He bestowed everything wonderful and marvelous, preceded by water.
Undoubtedly, as you, the lord of the clan of Diti, were performing that act of total self-surrender,
the sages and the gods together released a rain of flowers;
for all who partake in the universe were beholding this divine form of yours.
It grew higher and higher, having made the vessel of the cosmic egg its limit.
In this festival, Puṇḍarīkodbhava, out of excessive joy, sprinkled the tips of your feet—which had reached his own head—with water from his water-pot; that very water purified all the worlds.
Many beings moving through the air [rejoiced] in this celebration.
Striking the drum, the devoted Jāmbavān roamed through the world.
Meanwhile, the Daityas, having commenced their assault without their master’s permission,
were defeated when they encountered your followers accompanied by the gods;
for this one, who is Time itself, dwells before us, by whose power we were previously conquered.
"What use have you for battles? said Bali; with these words, they then reached Pātāla.

To the Daitya, who was bound by snares and addressed the Lord of Birds loftily, saying, "Grant me a third foot; are you not the Lord of the Universe?", [the Lord] spoke unshakably: "O Blessed One, place your foot upon my head."
Prahlāda, having approached him in person, honored and praised you.

"O Daitya! All that was ordained for the destruction of your pride has been accomplished; by your merits, may you possess a world, be victorious over the three heavens, and afterwards attain the status of Vāsava.
Furthermore, attain union with me. Thus did he favor Bali.
O Lord of the Abode of Vāyu, protect us, you for whom the best of sacrifices have been performed by the brahmins!

Long ago, during the unseasonable dissolution at the end of the sixth interval, when the great asura Hayagrīva had stolen the Vedas from the mouth of Brahmā as he was about to wake from sleep, it is said that [Viṣṇu], desiring to recover them, assumed the form of a fish.
At that time, as Satyavrata, the lord of Dramila, was offering libations into the river water,
you appeared to him as a certain small fish with a blazing form within his cupped palms.
Seeing you thrown into the water and looking about in alarm, the sage took you home in a water-vessel; and in a few days, O Lord, you filled the jar, the well, the pond, and the lake!
By the power of yoga and solely by your command, you were led from there to the ocean by the sage;
when questioned by him, you departed, saying to this one who desired to see the Kalpa, "Wait for seven days."
O Lord of Sages, when the day you had foretold arrived and the surface of the earth was inundated by torrents of water, you,
tossing about in the boundless waters, sought refuge in me along with the Seven Seers.
Then they ascended the Earth, who had assumed the form of a boat and was ready to carry out your command;
and as she trembled at their weight, you appeared once more upon the ocean in your full majesty.
Beholding you in the form of a fish, a hundred thousand yojanas long and possessing exceedingly lofty splendor,
the sages were delighted by your words and fastened the sun upon your towering horn.
Having drawn your boat, you traveled about, showing the divisions of the entire world to the circle of sages;
being praised by that best of men, you taught the supreme knowledge.
At the end of the eon, having seated those seven sages before you as before,
you rushed in anger toward Hayagrīva, while establishing that king Satyavrata as the Manu known as Vaivasvata.

Having struck down that Daitya, whose chest was pierced by Your own lofty horn, and having seized the Vedas, You gave them to Viriñci, whose heart was filled with joy; O Lord of the House of the Wind! May You grant me Your protection.
Ambarīṣa, the son of the king named Nābhāga— who was born from Nabhāga, the son of Manu known as Vaivasvata—
even though he cherished the entire earth surrounded by the seven oceans, found delight [in her].
With my mind always immersed in you and in those who are devoted to you.
O Lord! Since he performs everything solely out of devotion for your pleasure, you have not long delayed your favor,
by which you protect him even without his having to make a request.
You have cast forth the wheel with its thousand spokes.
Then, for the sake of worshipping Bhū (the Earth), he observed the vow of the twelfth day (dvādaśī-vrata) for a year in Madhuvana near the Yamunā;
together with his virtuous-minded wife, he performed that great observance.
Distributing worship among the twice-born, he [bestowed] sixty million cattle.
Then, on the day following the fast, at the conclusion of his worship of you, the sage Durvāsas arrived at his palace;
though he was habitually prone to causing distress, he was invited by the king to eat.
He went slowly toward the Yamunā, intending to perform his religious observances.
Then, due to the exhaustion from the long duration of the fast, the king— who was devoted to your welfare—
performed the breaking of the fast on that very day;
the sage, having attained divine vision, understood this.
Tearing out his matted locks in a fit of rage, he cast forth the Kṛtyā.
And seeing before him the Kṛtyā, bearing a sword and burning the world, the king did not tremble from his place;
for he beheld your Sudarśana [discus] intent on the destruction of those who harm your devotees.
Terrifying the sage with the fire of his magical spells, he pursued him.
Running through all the worlds out of fear and seeing everywhere even your wheel, he reached Viriñca; yet,
having been cast off [by him] with the words, "Who can overstep the wheel of time?", he fled.
He went to Śarva and indeed paid homage to you.
Having returned once more to the abode of Bhava and bowing to the Sage, he said: "O Rishi, are you not indeed my servant through devotion?
For knowledge and austerity are worthy of honor only when accompanied by humility."
O Infinite One! Go and worship only the feet of Ambarīṣa!
Then, having approached and grasped the feet of the sage, the king withdrew; he [the sage] bound his weapon [upon him].
When the wheel had departed, the sage bestowed all blessings upon him.
And praising your compassion, even though you have already granted your grace, he has come to you with devotion.
The king, having waited for the sage for one year without taking food himself,
and having fed that excellent ṛṣi until he was satisfied, then released him;
and after eating himself, he became even more firmly devoted to you.
And he attained union with me; O Pavaneśa, may you protect me!
Requested by the gods for the destruction of the ten-faced Rāvaṇa, the sage Ṛśyaśṛṅga performed a sacrifice for progeny for King Daśaratha of the Kośalas and gave him the finest milk-rice (*pāyasa*);
by eating that, the three queens of his also became pregnant simultaneously, and [from them] he was born.
You are Rāma, together with Lakṣmaṇa, as well as with Bharata and also with him named Śatrughna.
Bearing your bow and followed by Lakṣmaṇa, you went forth to protect Kauśika’s excellent sacrifice;
having dispelled the fatigue of the road through the peace of non-duality at your father’s word,
you split Tāṭakā with arrows by the power of the sage’s command for the protection of the sages.
Having obtained this collection of weapons from him, O Lord, I went to the sage’s grove known as Siddhāśrama.
Having routed Mārīca with arrows at the head of the sacrifice, slaying other rākṣasas,
making Ahalyā auspicious by the dust of his feet on the road, reaching the home of Vaidehī,
piercing the bow of the Moon-crested Lord, and having obtained Indirā herself as the daughter of the Earth;
You have established yourself in sovereignty, together with your three heroic brothers and their wives.

O you of lovely form! When the ornament of Bhrigu’s lineage, blinded by rage, had departed for Ayodhyā after transferring his own splendor [to the Sun], and while you were dwelling here happily with your beloved,
Bharata once went to the residence of his maternal uncle along with Śatrughna.
Father, it is said that your consecration, which was already undertaken, has been thwarted by the daughter of the Lord of Kekaya.

Desiring to go to the forest with your father, accompanied by the wives of the forest-dwellers and bearing your bow, you sent the citizens back on the road; then, having gone to the abode of Guha and donning matted hair and bark garments, you crossed the Gaṅgā by boat and proceeded further along the path toward Bharadvāja.
Having bowed down, we dwelt in great happiness on Citrakūṭa, the king of mountains, because of those words.
Having heard from the mouth of Bharata that your father had indeed gone to heaven while he was distressed by grief for his son, you were tormented;
having offered water to him, you placed your sandals upon the earth for Bharata.
Then, having bowed to Atri, you went to the forest, to the vast Daṇḍaka where the fierce Kāyāvas reside.
O, having slain the Daitya Virādha, you attained a beautiful state of well-being, like that of Śārabhaṅgī!
Having bowed to Agastya, who rendered the entire multitude of his enemies like birds with feathers stuck in a net,

you, desiring their welfare, received from the ascetics the account of what followed; and when the divine bow of Viṣṇu and the Brahmāstra had been bestowed by the sage, you consecrated Jaṭāyu, the friend of your father, on the path.
In the past, you joyfully embraced a young bride on the banks of the Godāvarī at Pañcavatī.
Having approached Śūrpaṇakhā, whose fortitude was shaken by passion, Rāma— his own self unable to endure her importunities—
dismissed her to Saumitri; and seeing her with her nose severed by him in a fit of intense wrath, Khara, Duṣaṇa, and the three-headed Triśiras rushed forward with hearts full of rage.
With the heat of his eyes unimpaired, he instantly struck down even ten thousand more arrows.

Following the deer-like illusory form of Mārīca—which had been dispatched by the Ten-faced Rāvaṇa when he was overcome by the news told by his sister—the lotus-eyed Sītā longed for it; yet, as she pursued it, he struck her with a volley of arrows.
Then Rāvaṇa carried her away, while her younger brothers were made to cry out by that very illusion.
Therefore, even though you were distressed within, you experienced an indescribable joy because of finding a means to slay him.

Then, while searching further for your slender wife who had been abducted by the Ten-faced one, Jaṭāyu departed for heaven after saying, "Your wife was taken by me for my own destruction. Thereafter, you performed the funeral rites for your friend; and seeing Śabarī on the shore of Lake Pampā, you slew Kabandha as he was seizing you.
Having reached the son of the Wind with a heart greatly rejoiced, [he cried: "Protect me, O Lord of the abode of the Wind!"
Having first brought about friendship with Sugrīva, you then,

by means of a pretext, struck down Vālī— who possessed incomparable strength and was intent on killing Sugrīva— after hurling the massive body of Dundubhi with your big toe and simultaneously shattering seven *sāla* trees with an arrow.
At the edge of Mataṅga’s hermitage, you spent the rainy season, your heart trembling with the pangs of separation.

Then, beholding that army of bears drawn up in battle array by Sugrīva— who had approached with trepidation at his younger brother’s urging— and seeing them bowing low in haste toward every direction in search of his beloved, he,
filled with joy, entrusted the message and the ring into the hand of the Wind-god’s son.
On every path, even on my own path, your beloved was pursued with great effort by monkeys.
Having heard news of you, he was overcome by a sudden, heavy surge of grief; then, upon hearing the words of Sampāti—
who had flown across the ocean after leaping from the summit— having seen Janakī within the city and given her his ring,
having crushed the garden and fought a battle skilled in destroying the Akṣas, that hero, enduring his bonds, confronted the Ten-faced one.
Having seen and scorched Laṅkā, Hanumān quickly gave you that crest-jewel.

You, having traversed the circle of the earth with the valiant host of monkeys led by Sugrīva and Aṅgada, and having crossed the ocean while being honored by the younger brother of the Lord of Night-dwellers (Naravāhana),
were listening in secret to the news of the enemy as reported by him; then, out of anger at the futility of your entreaties—
Through the words of the ocean-born [Vasiṣṭha], he attained the middle path by quelling the intoxication of the fiery power of the Agneya weapon.
Having constructed a bridge by means of hosts of monkeys who brought mountains from other regions,
and having crushed the demons with your own troops whose mountain-like claws and teeth served as axes and weapons, you,
along with your younger brother, displayed supreme valor on the battlefield against the conqueror of Indra.
Bound by the serpent-weapon with great force, you were liberated by the winds from the wings of the Lord of Birds.

There, the son of Sumitrā, perceiving Meghanāda— who prided himself on his treacherous ways— to be one whose life-breath was departing from the impact of the spear, took him by the nose with a gust of wind and deprived him of his life;
and having had his paralysis removed by the words of Vibhīṣaṇa during the disturbances caused by Māyā, he [confronted] Kumbhakarṇa.
You destroyed him who had arrived with his entire army shaking the surface of the earth and devouring it.

O Lord! Seizing the chariot and armor sent by Indra, engaging in combat with Rāvaṇa, shattering his formidable neck with the Brahmāstra, and accepting the unblemished bears who had died in battle and were restored to life by the power of Śreṇīvara—by you, O Deva! [the world was saved].
And together with the lord of Laṅkā, you went to your own city on the Puṣpaka chariot along with your beloved.
Delighted by divine consecrations, you sported for more than ten thousand years with Maithilī; yet, alas, alas, Śiva! when she was pregnant, you mocked her because of wicked rumors.
Having had Lavaṇa, the night-stalker, destroyed by Śatrughna, you then tormented the wretched Śūdra.
Having taken up residence in the house of Vālmīki, Sītā gave birth to those two sons of yours.
At the command of Vālmīki, whose sweet compositions were sung by your son in the sacrificial enclosure,
Sītā entered the earth when you desired her presence; and you, impelled by Time,
became the slayer of Saumitri for that very reason, and then yourself plunged into the Sarayū along with all your remaining servants.
O Lord! Having ascended to the celestial realm together with her, you returned to your own primordial abode, Vaikuṇṭha.

This incarnation of yours as a mortal is surely for the sake of instructing mortals; thus, through excessive attachment to the nature of desire, even innocent people may suffer the pain of separation.
Otherwise, O wielder of the discus, how could there be such a transformation of your mind when you have realized your own true self?
O you who are the singular embodiment of all beings! O Lord of the City of Wind! Shake off the torments of disease!
Formerly, you were born as the son of Atri through Anasūyā, named Datta;
while wandering at ease with your beloved, your mind free from the fatigue of attachment to disciples,
you were seen by the most devoted King of the Haihayas, who [offered] a boon to him—
Having first deprived them of their sovereignty and other privileges, you finally delivered them unto death by your own hand.
O Hari! In order to fulfill the boon granted to Arjuna and to destroy that entire race of kings who hated the Brahmins, as well as the burden upon the earth,
you were born from Jamadagni to Reṇukā in the lineage of Bhṛgu.
Among his sons, the youngest was named Rāma; he brought joy to his parents.

Having acquired the collection of traditional lore and being in his fourteenth year, he— though appearing somewhat like a Gandharva king— was, it is said, sent by the command of his father, who was agitated with anger toward his mother;
then, having cut her down along with his paternal uncles and brothers, he [acted] for the sake of pacifying his father.
He granted them the boon of the means for their livelihood, and your mother also granted a boon.

Then, having set out from his own hermitage for the sake of his mother’s joy— having brought down a celestial cow (Viyaddhenu) through his praise— and having worshipped the Lord of Gaurī on the Himālaya at the word of Bhṛgu,
he obtained from him that axe as well as great weapons and other gifts, and became the destroyer of the demons.
Having then obtained a friend, he reached the sage Akṛtavraṇa and returned to his own hermitage.
Arjuna, having gone out for the hunt, was honored by your father with wealth obtained from the divine cow; yet, upon returning to the city, he was again incited by the words of an evil minister and,
through that wicked-minded man, dispatched his counselor to purchase the cow, while the sage [Vasiṣṭha] obstructed him.
Vatsa was carried off by the wheel of the army of Goha, who, filled with rage, cast away his life.
Then Śukra, his anger stirred by the words of his father who had been restored to life, entered Māhiṣmatī together with his friend,
mounted on a chariot drawn by a bull and driven by a charioteer, wielding a bow and an axe that he had meditated upon and which had been placed within Mahodara.
With words, you praised the battle against King Madāśuṣi, who was like a calf.
The battle, which had expanded with seventeen myriads of sons and great commanders of vast armies, and which was a multitude of many friends,
suddenly became a heap of troops entirely shattered by your axe-like arrows.
The horse of Hehaya rushed toward you, while the remaining followers, fleeing in terror, perished.
Arresting him as he released many weapons and missiles from his thousand glorious arms— which had humbled the pride of the Lord of Laṅkā and sportively obstructed the waters of the Narmadā—
you, perceiving that even Viṣṇu was rendered powerless, joyfully recognized him as Hari.
You destroyed him as he was meditating, having abandoned all faults; he went to your supreme state.
When your father was slain by the sons of Hehaya who were filled with even greater indignation,
you beheld the hearts of those striking Reṇukā, and bearing a terrible vow, you— having summoned your chariot and weapons through meditation— slew the Kṣatriyas who had harmed the Brahmins.
Sweeping away the kṣatriyas from the earth with his axe throughout the circles of the directions.
Then, conquering the royal dynasties that restored life twenty-one times over, he satiated his ancestors with a great flood of blood at Samantapañcaka;
subsequently, while performing a sacrifice and bestowing the earth upon Kaśyapa and others, he again fought with Sālva.
Thinking, "Kṛṣṇa will slay him," you were restrained from battle by the princes.
Having laid down his weapons on Mount Mahendra while performing austerities,
and seeing the earth submerged as far as Gokarṇa by the ocean, he was entreated by the ascetics; then,
as he meditated upon the fire-weapon held in his bow, he [dried up] the ocean with the casting of his sacrificial ladle, terrifying it.
O Lord of the Bhṛgus, O Lord of Vāta, you who have cast out and uprooted Kerala, protect me!

O Hara, whose body is composed of intense bliss! Indeed, in the ancient war between the gods and asuras, there were those who, though severed by you, did not attain liberation due to the persistence of residual karma;
now, I am grievously oppressed by the burden of those sons of Diti who have been born upon the surface of the earth.
The earth reached Viriñca, whose station is sought by the gods who had already arrived before him.
"Alas, alas! Protect this earth, which is being crushed by the heavy burden of many wicked men and is about to fall into the ocean; indeed, ask these gods for my help!
Seeing the Earth thus rendered helpless by such profuse lamentations, the Creator [intervened].
O Hari! Having gazed upon the faces of the gods all around, he meditated upon you.
And the Lotus-born One said: "O gods! The words of the Earth are indeed true;
for the Lord of Lakṣmī is truly skilled in the task of protecting her and you.
Therefore, all of us, led by Śarva, shall go from here to the ocean of milk."
Having bowed to him, we praise him swiftly—those who together have reached your banner.
While those [devotees], their minds solely intent on meditating upon your feet, reached the shore of the milk-ocean stirred by the gentle breeze and gathered together, the Lotus-born Lord (Brahmā),
hearing your words in his heart, gladdened them all with these words:
I have not been described by the Supreme Self himself; let that statement be heard.
I know the miserable state of the gods and the earth due to fearsome kings;
therefore, with my entire self, I shall manifest in the Yadava clan to remove that [suffering].
May the gods be born in the Vrishni family, and may the celestial women come to the earth as portions of themselves.
"For the sake of my service"—thus did the Lotus-born speak these words of yours.
O Lord! Having heard Your words, which are like nectar to the ears, when all have departed with their hearts cooled and their souls satiated by the ambrosia of Your grace—
in that world-renowned city of Mathurā, which is indeed preeminent in merit due to Your presence— [we remain].
That king, the son of Śūra, married the blessed daughter of Devaka.
When the wedding was concluded, his brother Kaṃsa, honoring them both, set out on the road in a chariot as their driver; however, by your voice rising from the sky, he was told:
"Her eighth son will kill you, O most wicked one!"—and thus he was impelled to slay you.
Desiring to kill her with ease, he drew his slender sword as she drew near.
Seizing her by the hair, that evil-minded one did not release her despite Kṛṣṇa’s long consolations; yet, pleased by his words regarding the surrender of his own daughter, he then went home.
Likewise, although he had previously surrendered his first-born sister out of affection, he did not kill her.
O Lord! For even toward the wicked, a steady gaze of abundant compassion is indeed seen at times.
Then, with his mind alone, the sage Nārada said to the Lord of the Bhojas: "O Lord, you surely know that you, the Yadavas, and the gods are all asuras; do you not realize this?
That Hari, the master of illusion, will manifest for the sake of slaying you at the request of the gods."
Having heard this, he harassed the Yadus and slew the sons of Śauri.

O Mādhava! When the lord of serpents had attained the state of being the seventh embryo and was led away by Your power of illusion at Your instigation, You too, O Lord, whose singular essence is pure consciousness and bliss,
entered the womb of Devakī while being praised by the gods, O Blessed One!
Therefore, O Kṛṣṇa! having shaken off this mass of diseases, grant me supreme devotion.
O Lord of the nature of bliss! O venerable one! When your incarnation has arrived, the sky is filled with the masses of light radiating from your blazing limbs, as if by circles of dense rain-clouds.
Not obscuring [the world], the time of the rains has indeed shone forth.
When the quarters are cooled by the waters of the clouds, when virtuous people are rendered helpless in their longing for the fulfillment of their hopes,
and during the rising of the moon in the middle of the night—
You have appeared here in this world to cast away the afflictions of the three realms.
Even with a body that was but a child's, he displayed divine splendors through the radiance of his rising crown, bracelets, armlets, and necklaces,
and by being adorned with the conch, discus, lotus, and mace.
One should draw with black ink on a cloth in the house of the mother of the child.
By means of the various glances released from the bashfulness of Lakṣmī— who sports happily upon the surface of his chest—
may the ill fortune created by Kaṃsa be destroyed from that palace.
O Vāsudeva, you shone as if wiping away [all impurities]!
But Śauri, beholding with his own eyes that body standing at a distance— even though the minds of the assembly of steadfast sages were [otherwise] focused—
became moist with a voice faltering from the rising of tears of joy and horripilation.
He praised you, whose gaze is the essence of the nectar of lotuses.
O Lord! Be gracious, O Supreme Person! O you who are the sickle that cuts down the creeping vine of suffering! O you who possess the beautiful eye! O you who sport in the arts!
Remove my sorrows with your glances, heavy with compassion!
Thus, being delighted, he praised you for a long time with these and other words.
And you, the abode of compassion, whose body was embraced by the vine-like limbs of your mother drenched in tears, and whose virtues were extolled by hymns of praise,
awakened those two from their previous pair of births.
At his mother’s word, he assumed the guise of a human child.
Then, urged by you, that son of Śūra indeed set about to exchange [the infants] with the daughter of Nanda;
for he placed you, who cannot be held by the mind, into his hands, O Noble One.
Delightful with young kalahamsa birds upon its lotus-stalk-like thighs.
Then, at the house of Puṣpa, Yoganidrā was born;
she subsequently caused the citizens to fall into a sleep that eclipsed all other slumber.
What wonder is there here that even insentient things act according to your prompting?
The doors, though firmly fastened, opened of their own accord.
Then, with the remainder of the water shielded by his many hoods and with the path freely revealed by the light of his jewels,
he— truly the most blessed one— set forth while supporting you.
Therefore, O Lord, you who are this very one, destroy the force of my diseases!
O Lord, as this scion of the Yadu dynasty was departing, he beheld the daughter of Kalinda, with her mass of water rising high into the sky;
yet that collection of waters was merely a mass of serpents produced by Indra’s magical illusion.
In that very instant, he became immeasurable, like a surging flood of water.
Entering the cattle-pen, whose gates were thrown open and where the young girls who tended the cattle had fallen asleep,
he offered you to the birth-couch at her feet.
Carrying the deceitful maiden, he returned swiftly to his own city.
Then, the King of the Bhojas, distressed by the news of the birth announced by a host of soldiers who were rushing about as their sleep was shattered by the noise of your younger brother’s crying,
hurriedly rushed forward with his mass of hair disheveled.
As if delighted, he beheld the maiden in the hand of his sister.
"Surely this is the illusory power of that honey-thief who dwells in deceit," thinking thus, the elephant seized the young maiden— who was being embraced by her sister—
as one might pluck a lotus stalk from within a bed of lotuses.
This [person] has not ground your sister, who is unborn, upon a stone slab.
Then your devotee, suddenly as if liberated from the noose of death, immediately ascended into that intermediate state of form;
having descended to the lower realm, his eight arms expanded and quivered.
Having gone through the air to the great battlefield, she indeed shone forth.
"O most cruel Kaṃsa! What was gained by you when I was crushed? Let your own welfare be considered somewhere!
O Lord! Having thus addressed that wicked man, your younger sister departed."
Praised by the hosts of Maruts, she arrived upon the earth at her dwellings.
At dawn, however, having been addressed with the words of the Son of the Mountain (Nārada) by the King,
the proud Dānavas, led by Pralamba, Baka, and Pūtanā,
wandered fearlessly throughout the world, desiring his death.
What indeed is difficult for pitiless youths to accomplish?
Then, O Mukunda, while you lay upon the birth-couch of Nanda’s beloved in the cowherd settlement, your feet slightly raised as you cried out,
the women woke up and proclaimed the birth of a son.
Out of joy, what indeed shall I say? Alas, the entire Gokula is overwhelmed with agitation!
Oh, how wonderful! Yaśodā first gazed upon you with her eyes, which were captivated by your fresh black peas,
and then, with joy, she immediately made you drink from her own heavy breasts.
In this world, those possessing merit have conquered all by means of their touch, which captivates the mind.
Out of a desire for your welfare, what indeed did that Nandagopa, overwhelmed by a weight of joy, not give to the assembly of brahmins at that time?
Likewise, why did the cowherds not perform auspicious rites?
O auspiciousness of the three worlds! protect me here from disease.
Thereafter, having observed that Nanda had gone to the royal city— which was the abode of abundant auspiciousness— in order to pay tribute,
your father, who had learned of the efforts of Kaṃsa’s allies, spoke.
"O friend! Today the birth of your son brings me joy like the birth of my own son.
Having thus attributed the role of father to the Leader of the Vraja, he spoke to him with great affection.
"And here, there are hundreds of omens of ill fortune at the edge of your camp; therefore, depart quickly.
By these words of his, the leader of the army departed swiftly, out of fear for your misfortune.
At that very moment, O deceptive child, a certain woman of sweet form from Vraja,
whose hair was cherished by restless bees, approached your side.
Pūtanā, born of the race of night-stalkers, her consciousness stolen by the child she held,
took you up while the women of Vraja were momentarily reflecting, "Who is this here among the wives of the cowherds?"
Unable to resist him whose soul was captivated by the playful charms of her graceful gestures, she,
sitting within the house, offered her breast to you, who were disguised in a deceptive form.
Then, having climbed onto her lap without hesitation, you— provoked by the theft of your childhood playthings—
sucked at the circle of her breasts as if they were a large mango fruit, though it was tainted with bitter poison.
Sucking at your breast together with her own loathsome forms, she whose voice resembled the roar of thunder cast off her own terrifying body; having extended both her arms, she departed.
O Lord, when the cowherds were bewildered by hearing and seeing Your terrifying form with its fearsome roar,
did not the gopīs seize You as You sported upon their chests in the pastures of Vraja?
O Lord whose abode is the wind! You, who have been protected in many ways by young women through the very names of the worlds' ornaments—make me, your servant, free from disease.
Having heard the words of Śauri, Vrajeśvara, his mind filled with fear, was traveling along the road;
seeing a certain object upon which every tree had been utterly crushed, he sought refuge in you.
Having heard this account from the words of the cowherd women, all the cowherds, blinded by fear and wonder,
then beheld from afar that terrible body of the piśāca, severed by your axe and cast down.
Indeed, the thick smoke rising from her body, purified by being drunk by you,
caused doubt among the Agaru merchants as to whether it was from aloeswood, sandalwood, or guggulu resin.
"The fruit of contact with my limbs will not be far off; it shall happen to you all in an instant!
Uttering such words to the best of cowherds, you caused Pūtanā to exude a fragrance.

"It is a marvel that the prince was not killed by the Piśācī; it is a marvel that this was told long ago by Śauri!"—praising thus, the world of cowherds surely immersed itself in the aesthetic flavor of beholding your face.
Day by day, O Vāsudeva, this Vraja— its prosperity ever-increasing and its hundreds of auspicious signs undiminished through Your residence there— shone forth on all sides, thick with joy.
In their homes, who else has ever rejoiced so greatly every day, filled with tender smiles, mutual laughter, and conversation,
as they gathered for the performance of their daily duties while beholding you?
"Aha! The prince has cast his gaze upon me; Vatsaka has smiled toward me.
'Come, come to me!'—stretching out his hand, O Asha, what, what have you not done for the sake of these young women?"
Out of curiosity to touch your body, you were led from hand to hand by the cowherd women;
thus, you attained a beauty that rivaled a swarm of bees hovering over a garland of slightly reddened lotuses.
Feeding you at her breast as you rested on her lap, gazing upon your face while smiling—what state of being did Yaśodā not experience? O Hari, protect me from such calamities!
O Lord! Once, on your birthday, the Queen of Vraja—having invited her kinsmen, wives, and Brahmins—placed you near the kitchen and busied herself with the cooking and other tasks.
Then, from your vicinity, the crackling sound of bursting wood was heard mingled with the tumultuous roar of the boys appointed as your protectors, who were shouting out in terror.
Then, their breasts trembling from the agitation and exhaustion of hearing that news,
the women of Vraja beheld you on every side, situated amidst the terrible wood as it was being hewn apart.
"O, what has happened to the child? What has happened? crying out thus, Nanda, the cowherds, and the brahmins ran forward in haste;
and beholding you held by Yaśodā, they took heart, their eyes moist with tears.
"Who indeed is this person from somewhere or other? What is this vast wonder that the cart has been split apart?
There is no cause for this here," they stood saying, gazing at you with their hands placed over their noses.

"O Lord! We saw this child crying for his mother's breast; our lotus-feet were struck by him as he wept, and our minds were distracted by the thought, 'He is mine, he is mine!'—thus did those boys, the protectors, sing."

Then, out of fear, these words—so difficult to believe—were uttered by the boys who knew nothing of the truth, unaware of your power; they spoke thus because they had previously seen the Pūtanas and were somewhat apprehensive.
"What is this foot, crimson as a young sprout, that has been wounded? Or are these two hands, once as beautiful as lotuses, now withered?
Thus, their hearts rippling with spreading compassion, the women touched your body.
"O son, grant me protection today from falling into the waves of the Lord of the World's compassion! Thus saying, your father, his hair standing on end with joy, repeatedly embraced your garment.

It is said that Aniruddha, the enemy of the gods, came here intending to slay you, yet he was destroyed by you in such a way that not even his dust was seen; how then could he have surely dissolved into you, who are of pure essence?

O Lord of Amarāvatī! Having been specially honored there by the twice-born and having received their auspicious blessings, please dispel my affliction while enchanting Vraja with your own innate childhood charms.
Once, O Lord of Gurumahatpura,
your mother, unable to bear your immense weight as you climbed heavily upon her to carry you, cried out, "Alas, what is this? while laying you down upon her bed.
Seated in their homes, they meditated with apprehension fixed within them.
At that very distance, having heard the terrible roar,

that best of Daityas— whose form was like a whirlwind, who had filled the quarters with a mass of dust rising from his yawning, and who treated even the great mountains as mere blades of grass— [approached].
The one named Rta carried you away, you who steal the hearts of all people.
In this world of herdsmen, whose vision is struck by the darkness of unrestrained dust and who are unskilled in seeing anything at all—
alas, O young girl, why have you come into my presence?
Not seeing you, his mother wept bitterly.
Meanwhile, that foremost of Dānavas, his form dejected and his momentum shattered by the weight he had been forced to bear,
then recoiled at the sound of the dust raised by the wounded [elephant].
The cry of your mother spread throughout the cowherd settlement.
Upon hearing the news of your departure, the cowherd community led by Nanda approached their home and wailed in distress;
then a certain Dānava, seeking liberation, [approached] you, who grant liberation to all.
As you were not releasing it, it fell from the expanse of the sky.
Thereafter, the groups of cowherds, crowded with distress,
beheld his body, exceedingly massive, falling upon the surface of the stones outside— alas!— upon his own chest.
And you, being thus exhausted, are surely fit only for laughter.
Having approached you— who possess a bold laugh directed toward the wicked Danuja fallen from his body after it was crushed by the falling of the pressing-stones—
and who are striking [him] with your lotus-hand, [I bow].
The cowherds placed him there, as if they were placing a sapphire upon the finest of mountains.
Quickly seizing each one by turn, his limbs embraced and kissed by the cowherds led by Nandā as they rejoiced,
he was suspected by the cowherd women who desired to take him [into their own arms].
We pay homage to you, who have fallen from the lotus of [her] hand.
"Furthermore, what indeed shall we do? May Govinda alone, the remover of the distress of those who bow before him, protect our son!"—
thus did the mother, father, and others speak at that time.
O Lord, you alone have been entreated for the protection of the world!
O Lord of the abode of the wind, while thus shaking this Danuja who is of the nature of wind,
do you not likewise shake away my diseases born of wind?
Or what more shall I do, O Lord of the city of Anila?
I repeatedly entreat you for the complete pacification of all diseases.

O Lord! To perform for you, who are beyond all action, the purificatory rites according to the secret words of Vasudeva, the sage Garga—who knows the true nature of the internal day and night—has come to your home.
Then Nanda, his soul filled with joy, honoring that foremost of self-restrained ascetics,
spoke to him with words moistened by a gentle smile, his mind eager to perform the purificatory rites for him.

Saying, "O Noble One, this task must be performed with great secrecy because you are the preceptor of the Yadu lineage," Garga, his hair standing on end with joy, bestowed names upon you and your elder brother.
"How shall I give him a name— whether it be 'Thousand Names' or 'Infinite Names'?"— surely it was with these thoughts that you bestowed a name upon him in secret, O Lord!

The Sage, indeed, bestowed upon you the name "Kṛṣṇa," which expresses either your being the essence of existence and bliss through the roots *kṛṣ* (to draw forth) and *dhī* (intelligence), or your quality of drawing away the sins of the world.
And while reconciling other differences in names, you described Rāma and the others as your elder brothers,
yet you did not reveal to your father your own superhuman majesty.
"He who feels affection for all his sons does not suffer again from illusory sorrows;
but he who acts with malice shall perish"—thus did that best of sages describe greatness to you.
"He will conquer many more Daityas, lead his own kinsmen to the stainless state,
and you shall hear of his most pure glories"— thus did the sage describe your future glory.
"By this very [truth] you shall cross over all difficulties; remain steadfast in the mantra you have performed.
Thus did that sage describe you, saying "It is Hari alone," and so forth.
Now that Garga has departed, O Lord of Śrīmarutpura, you who are praised by Nandinanda and others, having aroused compassion within me, please cause me to emerge [from this state].
O Śabala! O Murāri! You two, adorning the various parts of the palace with the movements of your hands and knees—while your lotus-feet move, the tinkling of your beautiful anklets...
Possessing a curiosity to hear it, they moved gracefully with speed.
Gently smiling with their teeth slightly visible, their hair falling over their faces, the regions of their lotus-feet visible,
and marked by bracelets slipping from their wrists as they let go of the snakes;
Beholding the entire universe, it is the most excellent and supreme treasury of wisdom.
They followed along with the throng of people whose eyes were agitated by curiosity; laughing at something while making a sound, they ran on,
their lotus-faces turned back as they cast glances behind them.
O Vāsudeva, what curiosity would you not inspire?
Having fallen into the paths of rebirth and rising again smeared with mud,
they were being saluted with smiles by the sages in the heavens who were themselves free from stain; then they were quickly taken up with compassion by their two mothers.
Again and again you two were embraced and quickly kissed.

O Lord who feigns being a beast! Yaśodā, whose mind was wavering, is most blessed—blessed beyond measure—for she, holding you upon her lap as your heavy breasts flowed with milk, gave you her breast-milk; yet in the midst of that, there was the sprout of your charming smile.
Seeing her face, which was lovely with its budding teeth, he rejoiced.
Thereafter, moving about on foot and full of youthful restlessness, he played with the boys among the rows of forest dwellings,
running after the domestic parrots, cats, and calves.
Somehow or other, you were restrained by the cowherds who broke into laughter.
Wherever You, accompanied by Haladhara, arrived,
there the Gopīs fell helplessly with their eyes cast down;
they abandoned their household duties and forgot their children and servants.
O Destroyer of Mura! For a moment, they were constantly and utterly agitated.
Desiring ever-fresh butter given by the cowherd girls,
singing sweetly and dancing gracefully somewhere, he consumed the ghee offered by the compassionate young women.
In one place, you drank an excessive amount of milk that was not yet fully matured.
"Indeed, a request was made by me at the house of Bala; however, I shall certainly not make one here before women.
Having resolved thus, O King, why have you abandoned your begging?
And you stole the curd and ghee by means of a beautiful thief.
In the presence of your curd and ghee, the anger of the women of the cowherd settlements found neither space nor sorrow in their hearts;
having stolen even their hearts, you placed them in an ocean of joy.
O Lord of the House of Vāta, pacify my diseases!
Then, having seen the moon at the tip of a branch and repeatedly entreating your mother and father, saying, "It is a fruit," you raised your arm at their word; O Lord,
it is a marvel that the moon reached your hand— what can we say of its falling?
With its entire body filled by the circle of light, it first attained the state of Virāṭ.
Having for a moment immersed this father— who was seized with the agitation of wondering, "What, what indeed is this?"— in the ocean of Brahman,
[the Lord] again spread forth the illusion consisting of the delusion of his son.
O you who consist of bliss and consciousness! O you who pervade the universe! Protect me from disease!
O Lord! Long ago, while you were yet an infant lying on your back and nursing, a cowherd girl beheld the entire universe as your mouth opened wide during a yawn.
Furthermore, O Lord of the World, while you were once engaged in play with the children,
the boys, provoked by your deception regarding the gathering of fruit, said to you, "Eat earth."
"O All-pervading Lord! At the time of universal dissolution, you devour the earth, water, and all else;
fearing that pain might arise from even a soft morsel of food, your mother grew angry."
"O you of ill-behaved nature! Alas, my child, have you indeed eaten clay?"—to these words of your mother, O Lord, you long replied with a laugh, "It is false!"
"O, if you still harbor doubt despite this being determined by everyone, then tear open your mouth!
Thus rebuked by his mother, you tore open your face, which resembled a blooming lotus.
As if greatly satisfying his mother, who was eager to see even a mere fragment of clay,
he caused her to behold not only the entire earth, but all the worlds as well.
In one place a forest, in another the ocean, in another a cloud, and in another the netherworld;
in one place humans, in another demons, and in another gods—what was not seen then within your face?
How many times did she not behold you in her dream— lying in the ocean of milk, residing in the realm of the supreme Vaikuṇṭha, and yet existing within her own city as her very child?
Within the interior of her blossoming face, you—possessing a face of that very same kind—were clearly beheld by her once again; alas, you have thus brought about an infinite regress for all worlds!

Then, for a moment, charming his mother—who possessed a mind fixed on the ultimate truth—with his affection, he cried out, "O Mother, give me the breast! and added, "O Blessed One, O Child of wondrous power, protect me!"
Once, having approached your mother as she was churning curds, you,
out of greed for breast milk, came to her lap and drank from her breasts while she tried to ward you off.
O Lord! while you, whose face is a lotus sweet with a tender smile, had your bud-like breasts only half-drunk, your mother quickly went to catch the milk flowing from her own breast.
Alas, O Lord! With a mind overwhelmed by the weight of anger arising from the breaking of the vessel containing the half-consumed curd, you seized the churning-stick and shattered the bowl of curd.
Then, hearing that loud sound, his mother ran toward it;
she immediately saw the curd spilled upon the ground, spreading out like the diffusion of your fame.
Searching for you in anger after having sought you along the path of the Vedas,
that virtuous woman saw you being given butter to eat by Ota in a mortar.
Alas, seizing you, her lotus-face radiant with the dawning of fear, she— her countenance flushed with anger— quickly took up her girdle before her friends for the purpose of binding you.
O noble one, she desires you as her kinsman—indeed, that virtuous woman desires you as her very relative;
having fastened many cords of her girdle, she perceived you, alas, to be entirely two finger-breadths too short.

O Hari! Beholding her—gazed upon by her friends with astonished smiles and her body perspiring and languid—you, though your own form is eternally liberated, out of compassion indeed subjected yourself to bondage.
"Stay for a long time in the mortar, you rogue! she said; and when she had returned to the house, you remained there, hidden within the hollow of the mortar, having eaten the ghee she had offered.
"O All-pervading Lord, if you are easily accessible even to those bound by fetters, how much more so to me who am already bound by this [worldly] snare!
Thus praised by the gods, O Lord of the Wind, protect me from disease!
Having been praised with the cry of "Dāmodara" by the hosts of gods exulting in noble joy, you—
whose belly was soft— laying yourself of your own accord upon the mortar, looked toward two *kakubha* trees not far away.
The two sons of Kubera, known as Nalakūbara and the other as Maṇigrīva,
having attained prosperity through the service of Maheśa, sported for a long time while intoxicated and averse to you.

It is said that on the river Surāpagā, those two, intoxicated with wine and surrounded by many young women singing on the Surāpagā, were naked and intent on amorous play; Nārada, who is solely devoted to Your feet, beheld them.

Although they beheld before them their beloved’s face, which had already taken its place, their minds were blinded by passion; out of fear for them, the Sage spoke of tranquility for the sake of achieving peace through devotion to you—for without tranquility, whence can there be happiness?
"Having long beheld Hari, you two have attained the nature of *kakubha* trees; now you have reached your own proper place.
Thus addressed, those two, filled with a longing to behold Bhava, became *kakubha* trees at the edge of Vraja.

The two trees, worn out by age and shaken by the obstruction of the mortar, were long since withered; yet they were now further distressed and brought low by you, who moved so slowly as to encounter that very pair of tireless *indrādrū* horses.
O Govinda, at the very moment you split the pair of trees, a pair of Yakṣas of great luster emerged from their interior; at that instant, you too were honored with hymns of praise.

Even though he is devoted to another here, he will gradually come to you; for these two are indeed servants of Rudra, who have arrived at your feet through the grace of the Sage, having attained supreme devotion.
Then, while the circle of cowherds was fleeing in terror at the fierce sound of the trees being uprooted,
you, the bestower of liberation, released Nanda, who was looking toward the face of his own mother in shame.
"Alas, that child who was caught between the two trees is now unharmed by the power of Hari!"—while they were saying this, you were sent home. O Lord of Amarāvatī, protect me from the mace!

Indeed, the cowherds, being ignorant of your power, were filled with apprehension regarding the falling of trees and other such portents here in the cow-pen; fearing this multitude of calamities, they set their minds on departing elsewhere.
There, the eminent cowherd named Upananda sang: "Surely by Your very impulsion, it is known that to the west lies the enchanting forest called Vṛndāvana, which shines forth in splendor."
Having established that great forest as their primary cow-pen in an instant, the leaders of the Nanda clan then moved about,
followed by their mothers who were filled with the highest affection because of their connection to you.
Amidst the sounds from the hooves of the herds of cows lowing with discordant and unpleasant cries, the women,
drinking in the syllables of your playful conversation, did not perceive the length of the road.

O Lord! Beholding Bṛndāvana, with its multitude of trees headed by the Nandana, Prasūna, and Kunda, and enriched by the beauty of emerald-paved grounds and the lush splendor of its verdant lawns, you were filled with joy.
While all the cowherds were dwelling happily in their various new dwellings that had been recently completed,
you, mingled with the young cowherd girls, beheld the splendor of the forest and listened to its stories.
You beheld the Daughter of Kalinda, whose pure waters flow along winding paths, whose playful chatter is made by the cries of swans, and whose face is a lotus in constant bloom.
And you beheld Mount Govardhana, whose peaks touch the realm of Viriñci, variegated with gems that close their eyes at the sound of hundreds of peacock cries, and enchanting to the ear.
Then, together with the cowherd boys, you went all around to the edge of the forest;
there, here and there, you beheld that Kālindī river, winding like a single woman full of passion.
O Lord of the House of Samīra! While you were wandering with Rāma and the princes in such a cattle-grazing forest, eager for the movement of the herd of calves, protect me from disease.
Then, O Lord, you wandered through the enchanting forest of Vṛndāvana, which teemed with swarms of restless bees; eager to tend the calves along with the cowherd boys, you moved about,
O glorious one, accompanied by the wielder of the plow (Balarāma).
He held a flute made of buffalo horn and a staff, and his bodily luster was delightful to the eyes.
O Purifier, while you— who have established protection for the world and are caressed by the lotus-hands of Lakṣmī— bestowed your pair of feet upon Vṛndāvana,
what did not shine there as if filled with every prosperity, even the trees and creepers?
O Lord of Kamalā, [I offer] the waters, the earth, the lineage, the fields, and so forth!
Amidst the forest edge where the ulapa grass flourishes, cooled by gentle breezes,
upon the broad banks of the Yamunā and on the summits of Mount Govardhana, he indeed wanders with the Vṛṣṇi children, his charming flute-song resounding.
On a certain day, you beheld a Daitya in the form of a calf.
Beholding his tail quivering with impetuosity and looking on with a dejected countenance, his neck slightly turned as he watched for an opening,
[the king] then seized him by the foot and whirled him repeatedly high into the air.
Somewhere, you cast that wounded life into a great tree.
As that great Daitya, wicked by nature, fell at that very moment,
crushing the trees and mangling the forest with the force of his descent,
the gods in heaven, their throngs shimmering with joy, showered him with heaps of flowers.
O Hari! Then, indeed, they showered [flowers] upon your head out of joy.
When addressed by the children with playful curiosity, "Why does this most fragrant garland of flowers fall from above onto your head?",
you suddenly rose up from the circle of trees by hurling the demon upward.
"This is surely that very mass of flowers approaching slowly."
On a certain day, when the heat of the sun was becoming increasingly fierce,
you and others went to drink from the waters of the Yamunā;
there, you indeed beheld a crane with its wings fluttering, which had been forgotten [by you].
In its destruction of the weight of the mountains, it was like another Mount Kailāsa.

O Lord! When he, having rushed toward you while the cowherds were drinking water, swallowed that [poison] which resembled fire and then quickly vomited it up again, he went to crush you with the tip of his beak. At that time, O All-pervading One! [You struck him down].
And his sharp beak, ever-skilled at piercing the wicked, seized him and tore him apart.

When that Bakasura had departed for the abode of Death, the host of gods immediately went before Pūtanā— whether to behold her as she was born, or indeed as she was dead, or perhaps to wait upon even that vilest of men.
Scattering a multitude of flowers, you have come home from Vṛndāvana.
Having heard from afar the charming sound of the flute, the abode of the breeze was beheld by the womenfolk who approached quickly and gazed upon him with mounting joy;
he brought forth the blissful delight of his mother.
O Śauri, whose abode is renowned! Drive away my maladies.
Once, while you were exceedingly intent on consuming the forest together with the boys of Vraja,
you were surrounded by numerous circles of calves.
O Lord, you have emerged through those who are satisfied, by means of those who are satisfied!
The dust, which purifies the three worlds, has been raised from your two lotus-feet;
the great seers, with their bodies covered in horripilation, [have received it].
They wept, having held the festival of beholding you.
O Lord! While you were grazing your cattle on the ground covered with dense green grass, accompanied by the young princes,
the demon Aghāsura blocked the path for the sake of evil.
Suddenly terrifying, he assumed the form of one lying down.
In the forest, [beings] entered the mouth-cavity of the one whose body was like a great mountain and whose wide-open mouth resembled a cave,
out of curiosity to wander within it.
"O young boys, what [harm] can there be when you are at such a great distance?"
Out of negligence, one enters the belly of a serpent while the bodies of the cattle and their calves are boiling;
knowing this, O Lord, you too have entered it!
To quickly protect his friends who were without refuge.
When the great serpent, his breath suppressed as he writhes beneath you of expansive stature,
you will swiftly rend his circle of necks.
Liberating the animals and their keepers, he went forth.
O wonder! That great splendor arising from the mighty Asura, which had remained in heaven for a moment awaiting your arrival,
has now instantly vanished upon your departure.
Then, in the expanse of the sky, the gods danced and sang.
Then, followed by Kumāra and pursued by the gods, including the Lotus-born Brahmā, who were filled with wonder,
he proceeded as the day again reached its youthful state.
You celebrated a festival of feasting with your own people.
Placing his horn-flute upon his hip, holding a morsel of food in his lotus-hand,
he delighted the young boys with his sweet words.
You ate, being joyfully praised by the hosts of the thirty gods.
"O Lord of the World, praised thus by the best of the thirty gods: 'In this circle of cowherds, food that brings happiness is dear to you, just as the sacrifice is dear to the circle of gods.'"
O dweller in the city of the Maruts, protect me with your mace!

Then, observing that extraordinary excellence of yours— which had not been seen in any other collection of incarnations— and desiring to examine its nature beyond the perceptible, Brahmā [approached] for the sake of liberation from that evil.
Then, having spread out his illusion, he led away the herds of calves.
Seeing the herd of cattle rendered helpless by their calves, you, following the will of the Creator as if desiring to bring them back,
went at that time with only half your mouthful of fodder consumed.
The lotus-born Brahmā vanished after the princes had eaten.
Thereafter, you acted as a calf and then as a member of the cowherd community, taking the form of a carrying-sling, various household utensils, a flute, a buffalo, and so forth;
having sported for a long time in the forests as before, in the evening—
Then you, by means of your illusory power, manifested yourself in many ways within Vraja through that very illusion.

Bearing you alone in the form of the rope, the sling, the calf-rope, and so forth, you yourself again take the form of the animal, the cowherd boy, and the child; and even by means of those who are in the form of cows and in the form of cowherd women—
You were embraced with great joy by your mothers.
Indeed, out of the power of egoism, some living beings consider you their own and carry a heavy burden of attachment, thinking, "He is my son";
yet, having obtained you, who are the Self itself, as their son—
Neither the women nor the cows experienced even the slightest degree of joy.
Thus, at the end of a year, even your elder brother came to know you as one whose many forms were cherished by the entire host of cowherds through the weight of joy manifesting at every moment.
There is also a great distinction between you two and Brahman and the Self.
Seeing that the Creator had become dull-witted and bewildered during the rainy season— confusing the new and old cowherds—
he manifested fresh ornaments such as crowns and armlets.
The lords of the earth, endowed with four arms, resemble water-laden clouds.
Each one of them had limbs cherished by the goddess Lakṣmī, was reclining upon the coils of the lord of serpents as his bed, was delightful to the eye,
and had his eyes closed in playful slumber like the yogis headed by Sanaka.
The lotus-born Brahmā beheld you as you were thus intensely practiced.
Beholding that innumerable form of Nārāyaṇa and seeing himself as a servant everywhere, the Creator,
his heart submerged in illusion, became utterly bewildered.
At that time, you became one who held half a morsel of food in his hand.
Then, his intoxication vanishing, he repeatedly bowed to and praised You, the Lord of the Universe;
and as the Creator had departed for His own abode,
he entered His dwelling together with the joyful priests.
O Lord of Vātālaya! O All-pervading One! Protect me from disease!
O Lord of the worlds! Having passed beyond childhood and attained the charming age of paugaṇḍa, you joyfully left the calf-pen and set out to tend the herds of cattle.
O Lord of the City of the Winds (Kubera), this conduct of yours is indeed consistent with your previous undertaking;
for you began that very same task at that time when you descended to protect the lineage.
Once, while wandering happily at the edge of the forest, you beheld the splendor of the woods together with Rāma.
At the word of your friend named Śrīdāman, you went with joy to the forest of Dhenuka.
Then, when the thick grove of palm trees was shaken by the force of your words,
the host of fruits fell before him— both soft and hard— and the Dānava Dhenuka likewise fell.
Thinking, "I am intent on protecting the cows; how can I slaughter a cow today?
you, O elder brother, surely caused the host of gods to be obstructed by him as if out of such a consideration.

O Blessed One, together with your elder brother, you remained indifferent toward his servants who had arrived in the form of jackals; while sporting among the palmyra trees, you were then as free from attachment as if they were merely rose-apples.

When you were then destroying the flood of jackals, I believe that Varuṇa, being agitated by fear because of his sharing the same name, bestowed upon you the name "Jambuka," which is well-known in the Vedas.
"O Murāri, the fruit of your incarnation has been realized today! thus you were praised by the gods;
yet, laughing "Truly, the fruit has been realized here," you ate palm fruits along with children.
Having eaten those large fruits, which were dripping with honey and laden with fat,
you surely returned to the palace with your young sons, who were satisfied, proud, and carrying a flood of fruit.

"Killed! Killed is Dhenuka!"—as you approached, the people offered sweet fruits and hailed you, O Lord, saying "Victory! and "Live long! O Sovereign of the City of the Maruts, protect me from disease.

Formerly, a devotee named Saubhari, eager for service to you and performing penance for twelve years within the Yamunā, once beheld Garuḍa directly before him; he was filled with affection for a school of fish, while they themselves were greedy for food.

Observing that son of Tr̥kṣu, your mount, who was hungry and devouring some fish, he, with a mind distressed by heat, cursed him there, saying: "If you are a consumer of living beings, you shall also consume your own life."
At that time, Kāliya, eating his allotted portion from the enemy of serpents out of pride in his venom,
was cast into that unattainable water by You in anger because he had partaken of Your lotus feet.
On that terrible shore, the abode of the daughter of the Sun, trees were shattered by the force of the waves;
flocks of birds fell like falling clouds, and because of this, your mind became moistened with compassion.
Once, at that time, when you had left the wielder of the plow (Balarāma) and gone to the edge of the forest on the Yamunā,
the cows and cowherds, scorched by the fierce heat of the unrestrained summer, drank the water of the [Yamunā’s] whirlpools.

O Acyuta! seeing all those living beings perishing and fallen upon the surface of the earth, you, moistened with compassion, reached their side and instantly restored them to life with your glorious side-glances raining down nectar-like waters.
"What, what is this excessive rain of joy over all our limbs?"—thus the hosts of cowherds arose;
and seeing you before them and recognizing that work of yours, they embraced you, having witnessed your various powers.

And thus the cows, having regained their lives, were instantly filled with swelling joy; seeing you before them, they quickly surrounded you from all sides, shedding tears of delight and letting out low, rising sounds.
This horripilation all over our bodies and this certain swoon of bliss within;
this wonderful surge of joy at being called "Mukunda"—having been thus addressed by the cowherds, you were gladdened and honored by them.
In this way, you dispel the diseases even of liberated souls who are your devotees with the side-glances of your charming eyes;
O dweller in the house of the wind (Hanuman), you who are the very ground of such abundant compassion, may you protect me, who am sick!
Or else, O Blessed One, having resolved to ward off a most terrible serpent in the water,
you quickly went to a banyan tree on the bank whose mass of leaves had been withered by its venomous breath.
And having ascended with their lotus-feet, which were like fresh sprouts and possessed a charming luster,
they fell far into the waters of the lake, amidst a mass of violently tossing and formidable waves.
The river, its waters surging and trembling under the heavy burden of you who bear the weight of the three worlds,
suddenly submerged your hundred-bow-length form with a loud, crashing roar.
Then, amidst the weight of the roar of the waters in the cardinal and intermediate directions, agitated and whirled about in their depths,
the Lord of Serpents rose up from the water toward you, his mind blinded by unappeased rage.
Before them they beheld a serpent with many hoods, resembling a mountain of collyrium, a cloud of virulent poison fierce with sparks of blazing fire streaming forth from its thousand hood-tips.
That great serpent, with its blazing eyes, emitting fierce venom and heavy with the sound of its hissing breath, having bitten you—
who possess infinite strength— has now coiled itself around you, alas, while you remain motionless.
Then, seeing you not there while the herd of young cows was agitated as it went toward the bank,
and observing hundreds of ill omens even within the courtyard of the cowherd village, the cowherds departed for the Yamunā.

O All-pervading Lord! Seeing the condition of all beings who desired to cast off the burden of life, You, filled with laughter, quickly released the binding of Your serpent-hood and rose up with speed.
Then, having ascended the hoods of the king of serpents, she danced for you with her feet lovely and soft,
amidst the tumultuous jangling of anklets tinkling on her ankles and bracelets shimmering on her wrists.
The cattle-herders rejoiced, the sages were gratified, and the hosts of the lords of the gods showered flowers;
while you dance, O Lord of the House of the Wind, protect me from the diseases of those who have not conquered their senses.
O Lord, with your circle of earrings swaying gracefully, you danced for a long time upon the serpent;
while the celestial women sang in the sky, as beautiful as the drums struck by the immortals.
O Hari! Whichever head of his was the highest, you bowed down, leaving that one high behind;
then, crushing them with your lotus feet, you sported for a long time, making enchanting sounds with the clapping of your hands.

O Mādhava! When the Lord of Serpents, his multitude of hoods crushed and broken by you, sinks down in the water reddened by the blood flowing from them, his wives, overcome with grief, fall at your feet.

O Lord! Because their hearts had long ago been dissolved by the majesty of Your power as they had heard of it from afar, those women praised You, the Unrestrained One, with hymns that even the sages cannot reach through their paths of praise.

O Acyuta! With a heart overwhelmed by compassion that blossomed upon seeing the devoted glances of the multitude of serpent-wives, the Lord of Serpents, having surrendered his own body to you, bowed down before you and was granted life.
"The enemy of serpents will not cause hostility toward Ramaṇaka, which moves within the ocean in Vraja"—
honoring these words of yours with great respect, the Lord of Serpents departed together with his snakes.
Adorned with silk garments and radiant pearl necklaces bestowed by the wives of the serpent-king,
he met his kinsmen standing on the shore at the end of the day, who were drenched in tears mingled with the joy of women.
Furthermore, at night, when the multitude of people was unable to go to the cowherd settlement because of the darkness,
the forest fire, taking refuge at your feet, surrounded them on all sides as they slept there.
Then, as the herdsmen cried out in rising distress, "Protect us!
Protect us!", you, the Great Fire, rushed to protect them; what wonder is this indeed in your face?

O Lord! O Hara! Your yellow hue shines forth from your crest alone, and it is further manifested through your celestial activity; thus praised by joyful Paśupatis, remove my afflictions along with my sins!
O Lord, granter of desires! One day, you, the friend of Rāma, went to the forest, resplendent in your attire and surrounded by the sons of the cowherds as well as their cows.
Displaying the pure splendor of Vṛndāvana at his own will to Bala,
he went with the boys who carried bows to the Bhāṇḍīraka banyan tree while playing.
Meanwhile, a merciless demon named Pralamba, who desired your destruction and had assumed the form of a cowherd, approached you, whose arms were long.
Though knowing [the truth], as if not knowing, he formed a bond of friendship with him;
and near the banyan tree, they began a duel between two skillful wrestlers.

O Blessed One! Having divided the cowherds and formed a community consisting of Balabhadra and yourself, you then regarded the Daitya—who was terrified of your strength—as having come under the power of your own strength.
In battle, having defeated the enemy host with your imagined vehicle, you placed Śrīdāmā—who was most dear to you—upon it;
thus, though victorious, you manifested the state of being a servant to your devotees.
Thus, O Vibhūman, while many children were carrying and being made to carry [the load],
Pralamba, defeated by Rāma, carried him off from afar out of fear of you.
Seeing him carrying Balarāma— who had assumed a weighty burden— to a great distance,
