the Daitya resumed his own form, a form at which even Bala was struck with awe.
Beholding your face from afar due to the great height of the Daitya’s body, Rāma,
freed from fear, suddenly crushed this most wicked one with a firm fist.
Having slain the Dānava hero, you embraced Bala with affection upon his arrival;
meanwhile, a rain of flowers was showered by the hosts of immortals upon the heads of the two of you as you met.
O Lord who supports the worlds, who provides their sustenance, and who is their ultimate dissolution—by thus arranging [the universe], O You whose garment is the shimmering sky!
immediately remove the afflictions of Hari, having abandoned [all] time! O Hare! Hare! (O Destroyer! Remove the afflictions of Hari!
While you are eager to roam and linger in the crushing of hanging clusters of young trees, the cows wander at their own will,
grazing far and wide as they settle down out of curiosity for the grass.
They came upon a certain forest named Aiṣīka.
Those cows have come out from the interior of Vṛndāvana, which has not yet attained the cruelty of the summer heat, into this forest;
dejected by separation from you, they suffer under the scorching heat of the sweltering summer.
Agitated by the spreading and receding waters, they reached a state of paralysis.
Thereafter, O Śauri, having searched far and wide with your companions,
and seeing the herd of cattle exhausted from wandering in the dense forest and having lost their track, you quickly approached them from nearby to lead them back.
Alas, alas! As you departed, fire burst forth from every side.

When the fire blazes with a full halo, terrifying with its fierce roar, all those whose paths are obstructed and who are as if half-burnt, crying out in distress, "Alas, O Friend of the World! Save us! Save us!"—[all these] [are saved].
They have come to you for refuge, to you, the sole remover of suffering.
"Enough, enough! Close your eyes everywhere out of extreme fear!"—
at these words of yours, when they had closed their eyes,
where indeed was that forest fire, and where was that Munja thicket?
Alas, they immediately took refuge in the region of Bhaṇḍīra.
"Victory! Victory! What is this illusion of yours, O Lord?"—with these words of praise from them, his smile arose and he assumed various playful gestures;
once more, at the edge of the forest, he moved among the *pāṭala* trees and others.
In the experience of phenomena that are graspable merely as a collection of manifestations.
Like your own face, he bears aloft the heavy burden of heat;
like your lotus-feet, he dries up the mud within;
and like your arms, he projects a vast stream of radiant splendor.
He spent his time performing austerities in those forest regions.
Thereafter, with masses of clouds possessing a luster equal to your own body, and with the playful flashes of blossoming, pure lightning that serve as yellow garments,
you bring the time of the rains that bestows joy upon all who inhabit the world.
Dwelling at will in the caves of the mountains, you passed your time.
The Lord of Mountains, offering hymns through the fresh, melodious cries of flocks of peacocks, honors you who are seated within his deep caverns,
presenting a handful of flowers from the blossoming clusters of *kuṭaja* and *kadamba* trees.
O Lord! That Govardhana mountain offered itself, providing [shelter].
Then, honoring that autumn which had arrived— with its flood of pure water in the form of the hearts of your devotees— he wandered gracefully through the forests,
driving his cows to the edges of the stainless meadows of grass.
O Lord of the City of Wind, grant me physical well-being!

Beholding your body—tender as a fresh *kalāya* flower, yielding the milk of love, and enchanting all; composed of the bliss of the supreme consciousness of Brahman—the Creator and women alike become infatuated with it day after day.

O Hari! With their minds agitated by the god of love, the cowherd girls, gradually becoming intent on beholding you here and there, could not endure even your arrival at the forest at the break of day.
When you had departed, those fawn-eyed women, with their minds fixed on you, cast their gaze [toward you];
yet, hearing the sound of the flute from afar, they took delight in stories of your amorous play.
Having reached the edge of the forest, you too, standing upon the delightful ground beneath the lush trees with your feet positioned in reverse,
filled the flute’s pipe.

O Lord! Your flute-playing has manifested as that which shatters the host of sky-faring goddesses pierced by Māra’s arrows, renders the assembly of beasts and birds devoid of emotion, and even causes stones to melt away.
With fingers like petals trembling over the holes of the flute and feet like tender shoots moving to the rhythm of the beat—
that very form of yours, though standing beyond their sight— alas, the women of Vraja fainted as they contemplated it.
Seeing the sky-dwellers, birds, wild animals, and even the beasts who fearlessly gazed upon your body,
and seeing the forest devoted to your feet, they surely praised it as "most blessed, most blessed."
"When shall I drink the nectar of her lower lip? Or perhaps that which remains from the essence once tasted by the flute?
"Alas, it has been cast far away by one of evil intent! Thus, agitated, these women repeatedly fainted again and again.
Furthermore, O Lord, every day, because of the favor born from their hearts being your source, these women—
helpless due to their bound passion for you— constantly fall here into a state of confusion regarding their duties.
Passion indeed arises from one's own nature; through effort, it may or may not lead to the means of liberation.
Yet for them, that one [passion] and those two [liberation and effort] were already obtained. O Lord, protect me, whose fortune is my fortune! Do not let me die!
With hearts afflicted by love and desiring daily to serve Your two feet,
those tremulous-eyed women worshipped Girijā upon the sandy banks of the Yamunā.
Delighting in the story of your name, the Sudṛśas arrived together at the river in the morning and worshipped with hundreds of offerings, thinking, "May Nanda’s son become our beloved."
Having observed those tremulous-eyed women who had maintained their vows for a month, you,
tender with compassion, approached the riverbank with the desire to show them favor.
Having completed their ritual observances, those women then cast off their own garments at the edge of the bank;
distracted by their play in the waters of the Yamunā, they were filled with shame upon beholding you before them.
Then, as the women bowed their faces with modesty,
he seized the mass of cloth held near them and swiftly climbed onto that branch of the tree.
"Come here first, O fair-eyed ones, and let your garments be led away according to their respective order"—
when you spoke thus with a playful and gentle smile, the women were utterly bewildered.
"O young soul, live long! Why do you not subdue us, your maidservants?
O lotus-eyed one, when thus addressed, you offered nothing but a smile."

Having ascended the bank, those pure women, with palms joined in reverence, beheld their own celestial destinies; then, with joy, they offered all their garments as a gift and spoke these words once more:
Surely you know our desire; as those worthy of speaking, you have given the fitting reply here when the women said, "The nights on the banks of the Yamunā are filled with moonlight."
Having overheard the honey-dripping words falling from your mouth,
O friend, those fawn-eyed women looked again and again at your lotus-face out of affection, and then slowly departed for their homes.

O Hari, who, having thus favored the cowherd girls, now wanders as before among the peaks of Mount Govardhana; O you who are cool with compassion, quickly remove for me the entire multitude of my ailments!
And then, having gone to a forest very far from Vṛndāvana with the cowherds and their herds of cattle,
you indeed bore within your heart a firm resolve to bestow grace upon the multitude of the bodies of the most devoted twice-born ones.
Then, beholding the young calves in the shelterless forest interior, hungry and distressed by thirst,
he sent them from afar toward the twice-born who were intent on sacrifice, to request [milk] for them.
Then, after those [other] boys had departed, having uttered their names, they requested food from Odana;
yet those best of Brahmins, though firm in their learning, acted as if they had not heard, and being deaf to the request, they said nothing at all.
Indeed, the children, their minds distressed by neglect, returned; for this was only right regarding those who perform sacrifices.
Indeed, those Brahmins have long been devoid of devotion; how indeed could they offer what is devoted to you?

"Announce me to the householders; let these women, overwhelmed with compassion, give me food. Thus addressed by you with a smile moistened by affection, those boys went and made their request to the wives.

When your name was uttered, they became agitated with excitement; taking up the four kinds of flavorful foods, and having long maintained their intent to gaze upon you, they arrived swiftly even though restrained by their own attendants.
With their hair adorned with trembling peacock feathers, their earrings shimmering upon their cheeks, and their glances moist with emotion,
they gazed at you as you stood there, having placed your arm upon the shoulder of a friend.
And at that time, a certain woman, having set out to approach you, was taken by the hand by her husband, a performer of sacrifices;
thinking of you at that very moment, she immediately entered into absolute liberation—oh, how fortunate she was!

Having taken food and shown them favor, you sent them home while they were still yearning for contact with your limbs; yet, O Lord, upon seeing these women being dismissed for the sake of the sacrifice, you did not feel reproach toward them.

O Lord of Marutpura! Having examined their own faults among women and observed their devotion, those twice-born ones who investigate further and have awakened to reality have praised you; therefore, ward off my diseases.
Once, O Śauri! observing the cowherds who had prepared the wealth of materials for a sacrifice, you— desiring to uproot Indra’s pride,
though knowing these [cowherds] were as gentle as Nanda and the other herdsmen through their humility— [acted].
"O Janaka, you did not ask: 'Who is this person, and what is the purpose of your endeavor?'"
Nanda said to him, "O son! Surely you must perform the sacrifice for Indra year after year;
for that sacrifice brings happiness through rain, and everything on this earth that sustains mankind depends upon the rains."
Especially for us, cattle indeed live on grass and water.
Having heard these words of his father, you replied with this poignant speech: "Fie on us! That it is said 'the rain is produced by Indra'—is that true?
For it is indeed unseen destiny that creates for living beings the rain appropriate to their needs."
In the great forest, do trees offer any tribute whatsoever to Indra?
This much is certain: that which is our family wealth here on earth, this Bali, is fit to be offered as sustenance to the Lord of the Mountains;
for surely the gods of the earth are superior even to the celestial gods upon the surface of the world.
Therefore, you have declared to your own people that even they are to be propitiated.
Having heard your words, those herdsmen, filled with great respect,
honored the foremost of the twice-born and offered abundant tribute to the mountain king;
bowing deeply with profound reverence, they performed circumambulations around him.
O you whose self is the mountain, you formerly accepted the entire offering from the Ābhīras.
And you said this to them: "What falsehood have I spoken here?
Surely the Lord of Mountains enjoys his own offering with his own body;
and this Gotra is capable of protecting [us] even when the Enemy of the Gotra is enraged."
When it was said that they were all together, all those who dwell in Gokula rejoiced.
While those who had gone forth from Vraja, filled with joy at having met you, were returning to their home,
he heard of the disruption of his own sacrifice;
though he knew you were there, his heart was overwhelmed by excessive passion.
Even Śakra, the lord of gods, did not tolerate the arrogance you have fashioned for yourself.
"Even though he has attained human form as the slayer of Madhu, if he displays such insolence toward the gods, the majesty of the assembly of the thirty deities is utterly lost;
therefore, I shall destroy the fortune of this wretched beast."
It is said that Maghavan, that treasury of insolence, has set out to conquer you.
Sending forth clouds from the sky to destroy your abode,
bearing a thunderbolt as his vehicle, and moving with the speed of a cloud-elephant,
he set out, ridiculed by others such as Antardahana and Marut.
O Lord of the three worlds, whose mind does Your Māyā not delude?

Having reassured the cowherds by saying, "If even the enraged Lord of the Gods were to come, we would certainly remain free from fear through the compassion of the twice-born and the grace of the mountain," he dwelt there,
reflecting, "Alas, why has the Mountain-Cleaver not yet arrived?"
O Lord of the Maruts' abode! O Enemy of Mura! Drive away my pains.

Indeed, at that very moment, the clouds above the Vraja region— shaking the horizons with their unimpeded thundering and having attained a likeness to your own limbs through their beauty— were beheld by you.

While the herds of cattle were being punished in every direction by the falling torrents of water from the vast hands of the enraged Hari, they cried out to you, "Protect us! Protect us! from the blows inflicted by him.
O Ajita, hearing these words, you said, "Do not be afraid."
"O Lord! In this world, who indeed could obstruct the destruction of the enemy of the *gotra*—whether it be one's family, lineage, or deity? What doubt can there be in this matter?
Thus spoke he with a laugh, as he [lifted] Mount Govardhana.
O child, quickly uproot this tree from its very roots with your two arms!
Thereafter, while this best of mountains was being lifted up,
[the Lord] saw from afar, in a sandy and soft region where the heat had been warded off,
the cowherds and their cows mingled with their attendants below.
He placed the mountain upon his lotus-like hand with a double support.
It is a place where the mountains are held steady by young girls, where playful sport is enacted even by companions, and where the peacocks are restless with their cries;
it is a place where cows, having gathered close together, scratch one another with a single hand.
When he was thus satisfied, all the cattle-herders sought his favor.
"The mountain here is truly immense, yet he holds it for a long time upon his left lotus-hand!
Thus did the cowherds, beholding you, exclaim, "What indeed is this miraculous power of the mountain?"
"Aha! What audacity this boy displays! With his arm trembling, he shall bring down this mountain!"—thus reviling you, Hari rained down fierce torrents for a full day.

O Lord! While you remained motionless, even as the mass of clouds had shed all its water and was being carried away by the wind, the Lord of the Maruts, his mind filled with apprehension regarding you, rushed forward.

O Lord! When the burden of the rains had then subsided and the herd of cattle had departed for their pastures, you were embraced by the joyful cowherds upon the earth, which was laden with its weight of mountains.
"In former times you indeed supported the very earth; what effort could there be for you in lifting up the mountains?
Thus praised by the gods, O Lord of Kumalā, O Abode of the Guru, protect me from disease!
Having beheld your lofty power manifested in the lifting of the mountain and other such deeds, all the cowherds,
recognizing you as the Lord of the Universe, asked Nanda about your birth.
Your power has been proclaimed by your father to his own circle;
our affection for you, already great before, has now increased into a weight of profound respect.
Then, his realization of the ultimate truth awakened by that humiliation, the king of the gods, together with the celestial cow,
approached and— his pride destroyed— praised you after touching your lotus-feet with his jeweled crown.
Sneha bathed you with fragrant waters from the *stūnas*, while Indra, filled with joy, also consecrated you with the divine waters of the Gaṅgā brought by Airāvata, all bearing the name Govinda.
When you, the Lord of the three worlds, were consecrated as the Lord of Gokula, the cowherd settlement attained,
through your power, a splendor unattainable even in the realm of Vaikuṇṭha.
Once, while bathing at dawn in the Antaryamunā river, your father was led away by a servant of Varuṇa;
you went to that city of Varuṇa to bring him back, assuming a mortal form for that purpose.

Having been honored with great haste by that lord of the waters, you accepted your father and returned to your own home at that very moment; thereupon, your father related his adventures to his own people.
O Viṣṇu! Having determined you to be Hari and seeing these beings whose thirst is fixed upon beholding your feet, you have shown them that supreme state which is difficult for others to attain.

O Infinite One! Those very groups of cowherds who were long submerged in the great ocean of liberation, filled with a surging flow of the essence of supreme bliss, have indeed been raised up by You alone.
O Lord, just as in the Karabhadara incarnation,
where You manifested Your own state— which is otherwise unattainable— to those possessed of devotion;
so too here, O Supreme Self, You have indeed appeared in person in the form of a beast.
O dweller of Pavanapura! Protect me from all diseases.
Having told the Gopī folk at the conclusion of their observance that it was the festival of Marut, you then set out to accomplish it,
cooling the entire region with your dense moonlight.
He filled his flute at the edge of the forest on the Yamunā.
O Lord! Hearing the sound of your flute, which causes the entire expanse of the world to vibrate with rising circles of resonance, the young women—
They experienced such an indescribable delusion of mind.
Those lotus-eyed women, devoted to household duties, attached to their sons, and intent on serving their husbands,
abandoned everything once they were enchanted by the sound of the flute.
O you of lovely form, we have come together to this forest region.
Some, while putting on their own body ornaments,
having heard the sound of the flute, left their adornment half-finished;
indeed, they have come to you adorned in that very state.
Those very [stars] shone brightly for your eyes.
O Lord Mukunda! A certain woman, wearing a necklace upon her hips and a girdle around her neck, has come before you;
she has surrendered the beauty of her own loins to you.
He spoke clearly, appearing especially like one who was blissfully deluded.
A certain woman, her bodice clinging once more to her breasts,
approached you with a burden of incomparable affection, unobserved by other women due to her confusion.
Like a water-vessel for the purpose of the royal consecration ceremony.
O Lord! some women, indeed unable to emerge from their homes, having meditated upon You alone with firm resolve in their hearts,
cast off the body and became one with the nature of the bliss of supreme consciousness.
Indeed, these most blessed ones have entered into you, the Supreme.
Remembering you as their lover rather than as the Supreme Self,
women have attained the state of the Paramahaṃsa in an instant;
therefore, somehow [remember] you, whose body is the manifest Supreme Self.
Carrying the nectar in my heart, may I attain it without weariness.

With your face moistened by a charming smile and your compassionate gaze, you— the boundless ocean of splendor— are being gazed upon from all sides by the beautiful women of Vraja who have approached you.
O sole heart of the universe! O Supreme Lord! Remove my diseases.

Although she had resolved to grant the desires of those beautiful women who had approached her— women rendered helpless by the falling arrows of the flower-weaponed god— she nevertheless spoke to them as if with reluctance.
To cause the assembly of sages situated in the sky to hear it, you have proclaimed the dharma of a virtuous wife;
indeed, your words are righteous, yet your conduct is not to be trusted, for you are stainless.
Hearing those contrary words, those fawn-eyed women became deeply distressed;
"Do not, do not, O Ocean of Compassion! Do not abandon us! they lamented for a very long time.
O Murāri, your mind overwhelmed with compassion by their weeping and lamentations,
you proceeded with them to sport at will upon the banks of the Yamunā.
On the pathways along the banks of the Yamunā, beautiful with moonbeams shimmering like water-jars,
you sat down upon a seat prepared by the upper garments of the cowherd women.
With very sweet and playful conversations, with the grasping of hands, with the delights of kissing,
and with the embrace of firm embraces, you threw the world of women into a state of agitation.
O Lord! On the day their garments were taken away, you granted those beautiful-browed women—who had hearts overwhelmed by passion—the very garments they had promised to them.

O Son of Nanda! Having embraced you—who have blossomed with even a trace of dharma, whose lotus-face smiles as gently as a *kunda* flower, and who are the most beautiful in the three worlds—the young women are filled with joy.
In separation you consist of embers, yet in union you consist of aesthetic passion;
that in this union you are once again utterly composed of embers—that is the wonder!
O Lord of the City of Wind! May I propitiate you, whose soul longs for the beautiful embrace of Rādhā’s lofty breasts; please pacify all my maladies.
Having attained the play of sexual union with you, whose essence is the surging nectar of supreme bliss,
those lotus-eyed women reached a state of great intoxication, attaining an infinite weight of bliss.
"He, the Lord of Ramā, who delights the minds of all, has merged into me through his illusory power (māyā)!"—
thinking thus, O Govinda, all those women, filled with pride, beheld you as you vanished from their sight.
O Murāri! Having taken that most beloved cowherd maiden named Rādhā—who was free from pride—and having engaged in private dalliance with her, you have gone far away.
Then, O Blessed One, when you had vanished, those lotus-eyed women, filled with grief, gathered together and,
searching for you in forest after forest, fell into boundless despair.
"O mango tree! O campaka! O karṇikāra! O mallikā! O mālatī! O young creepers!
Why was he, the sole thief of our hearts, not looked upon by you? Thus did they lament, their minds entirely devoted to you.
"O friend! This lotus-eyed one is right before me!"—speaking thus in agitation, a certain woman, seeing you with her eyes of contemplation, doubled the distress of her companions.
Identified as being of your own nature, they indeed imitated your activities on the banks of the Yamunā;
yet, searching for you once more, they beheld Rādhā likewise separated from you due to her pride.
Then, searching for them together throughout the forest until the descent of darkness, they were reunited once more at the edge of the Yamunā’s bank; they lamented deeply and sang of his virtues.

O sole ocean of compassion! To the women of Vraja whose minds were overwhelmed by such distress, you—whose very nature is to enchant even the enchanters of the three worlds—manifested yourself with a gentle smile.
Beholding you, who are as beautiful as the moon, at that time, the slender women suddenly—out of the great weight of their joy—what did they not do? O Māruteśa, protect me from disease!
O lotus-eyed one! At the mere sight of you, the cowherd girls, overflowing with joy, stood motionless before you as if drenched by a stream of nectar.
Thereupon, a certain woman, suddenly and without hesitation grasping your lotus-hand,
placed it against her full breast and stood for a long time covered in horripilation.
O Lord! In the past, she, overflowing with joy, wrapped her tender arm around the interior of your neck, as if restraining the vital breath emerging from your throat.
A certain amorous woman, devoid of shame, having received from your lotus-face the chewed betel nut and placing it in her own lotus-mouth, has attained the fulfillment of her desire.
"O pitiless one, you have departed from the forest, abandoning me; who could possibly touch you?"—thus were you gazed upon with tearful eyes by that single woman as she spoke in anger.

Thus, accompanied by the cowherd women who were overflowing with joy, you arrived at the bank of the Yamunā and shone resplendently upon a seat fashioned from their soft breast-cloths, glowing with saffron.
"How many kinds of compassion are there? Some possess the dawning of mercy toward all; some toward those who have taken refuge;
and a few such as you show it even toward those like me"—thus were you addressed by the cowherd women.
"O maiden! Do not suspect any hardness in me, who am tender with love;
you yourself said that I did this in order to comply with the wishes of your heart."
"O beloveds of Jīva! Listen: no one is as dear to me as you.
Therefore, enjoy yourselves here during these delightful nights without restraint"—such was the speech of the Lord.

O Lord of the city of Gokula, protect me from disease— [I who am] filled with curiosity for the Rāsa dance, having sported together with the women of Vraja, whose hearts were overflowing with joy at these words.

Her mass of hair was adorned with a spreading array of peacock feathers; her ears were graced by swaying crocodile-shaped earrings; she was lovely with necklaces, forest garlands, and thickly applied fragrant unguents;
she was elegantly dressed in yellow garments and a bodice, and her feet were adorned with shimmering jeweled anklets.
O Lord! We indeed perceive Your form as adorned by the rāsa-sport.

Just then, O Beloved of Indirā, as you were wandering between a circle of young women who had completed their adornments— their breasts encased in bodices and their cheeks shimmering with jeweled earrings—
you passed between a pair of all-beautiful maidens.
Thereafter, O Lotus-navelled One, You performed the charming *rāsa* dance-play.
O Vāsudeva! Having perceived from afar the fragrance of the rasa of your Rāsa-sport as it manifested here— having heard of it from Nārada and being agitated by curiosity—
you were surrounded by hundreds of graceful, playful women adorned with fine attire and ornaments.
Then, the circle of gods arrived simultaneously from the sky with great speed.

It was enchanting through the blending of the sweet melodies and passionate rhythms produced by the sound of flutes, while the charming synchronization of cymbals was created by the gentle descent of her feet;
meanwhile, her bracelets jingled upon her hands, which were repeatedly raised with lotus-like palms hanging down from her shoulders.
Enjoy the splendor of the rasa-play, wherein the silken garment on her rounded hips is swaying.
Then, amidst a dance performed with a sweet voice rising in high and low pitches by followers created through faith, and with graceful bodily movements and jeweled ornaments swaying,
the host of gods in heaven, their eyes wide open, rained down flowers in great joy.
As if dissolving into you, who are composed of consciousness, the entire family along with their daughters-in-law fell into a swoon.
Then, a certain cowherd woman— her slender vine-like body drenched with sweat,
her eyes half-closed in exhaustion,
and her hair disheveled— leaned upon the shoulder of her beloved; another, possessing the fresh fragrance of the essence of sandalwood, [did the same].
Through deception, he kissed your arm, which was covered with sprouts of horripilation.
A certain woman, placing her own cheek against yours— thereby jostling your earrings—
attained the nectar-like flavor of the betel you had chewed; for you are the abode of Lakṣmī’s pastimes, the beauty of the world, appearing thus amidst your dance.
Having obtained you, did women not indeed experience a state of intoxication with supreme joy?
O Lord! The singing has indeed ceased, and the orchestration of instruments has gradually come to rest;
overwhelmed by the essence of the bliss of Brahman, the women in the assembly danced alone, unaware even of their head-dresses, their tresses, or their bodices.
Even the cluster of luminaries suspended in the sky—what more shall I say?
O Lord! Having dissolved the universe at the end of the eon and having completed Your divine play,

[You appear] before the wives of the Paśus— their hearts unable to endure the god of love, their bodies made beautiful by the slight drops of perspiration from their limbs soiled by the exhaustion of amorous sport, and impelled by their own past merit.
With your form thus perceived, you have brought about the supreme festival of the heroes of Māra.
O Lord, you indeed sported charmingly with your beloved circles of women, who were exceedingly cherished and agitated by various amorous pastimes;

O King, you stood within the cave before this devotee with your most graceful form.
Seeing that descendant of Ikṣvāku— who was dispassionate toward all royal pleasures, who desired only your grace,
and who was free from longing even for a multitude of boons— praising you while crying "O Lord!", [Śiva] rejoiced;
and having granted him liberation, which is equal to devotion and which instantly shakes off all impurities, he bestowed it upon him.
For he then requested that asceticism be considered a duty for the purification of violence, in order to conform to worldly opinion.
Thereafter, having gone to Mathurā and destroyed the army brought by the Yavanas, he was again obstructed on the road by the forces of the Lord of Magadha as before;
yet, having granted him his final victory out of pride, he fled.
O Lord of the Wind-god's abode, you who have gone to the city of the ocean, protect me!

While situated in the midst of the ocean, you adorned the new city with your body of accumulated radiance— a city whose craftsmanship was increased by Viśvakarman and which possessed all splendors bestowed by the gods.
When the Lord of Wealth gave his daughter Revatī to the wielder of the plow (Balarāma) in accordance with the decree of fate,
the Yadavas, filled with joy, together celebrated a magnificent festival of exultation.

Then, O Lord, your brother, resorting to his own darkness, would not himself give the daughter of Vidarbha, Rukmiṇī— who was indeed devoted to you— to the King of Cedi, taking refuge in that which is unrighteous.
The young girl, who had long cherished affection for you, was suddenly overwhelmed by the fear of her desire being thwarted;
she dispatched a brahmin to inform you of her own distress, brought about by the god of love.
The son of the twice-born also quickly arrived at your city, which is indeed difficult for the wicked to approach;
honored with respect by you, he personally attained joy as his affliction was removed.
And he said to you: "In Kuṇḍina, the princess Rukmiṇī indeed shines;
for she, longing for you and having lost her own composure, has sent me here."
"I was already captivated by your virtues long ago; now indeed the King of Cedi is carrying me away.
O Abode of Mercy! Protect me!"—thus she spoke, O Sole Lord of the World!
"If you abandon me, who am without refuge, I shall immediately give up my very life"—
by these words of your daughter, your compassionate heart was made exceedingly distressed.
Then you said to him: "O friend! My pain from love is even greater than that.
Therefore, O dear one, having approached the presence of the king, I shall carry off that beloved lady with her dark eyes."
Then, accompanied by him who was filled with joy, he quickly reached Kuṇḍina in his chariot;
O Lord of Marutpura, may you, my venerable one, dispel the multitude of all my misfortunes.
Accompanied by his army and honored by Bhīṣmaka, you entered the city;
she, her passion aroused, quickly bowed down to the son of the twice-born who spoke of your arrival.
Beholding your body, which is beloved by the world, and hearing of the prince’s conduct,
the night passed away in tears and lamentations from the city-dwellers who were overcome with profound grief.

Thereafter, the moon-faced Śivā, radiant with auspicious ornaments, having offered her life to Bhava, went forth from her own city ahead of him, surrounded by excellent warriors, in order to pay homage to [Śiva].
Having approached and reverently worshipped the Daughter of the Mountain, the young women fell at her feet and repeatedly entreated her, saying, "May she fall only for you."
Having observed the royal assembly crowded with curiosity and you standing there silently,
the princess emerged from the temple of the Mountain-Daughter, most beautiful and illuminating the quarters of the horizon with her splendor.
O Lord, at that time, when the entire assembly of kings was rendered helpless by the splendor of her form which enchants the world,
you too were slightly intoxicated by that charming woman through the casting of her side-long glances.

"O moon-faced one, where will you go?"—thus addressing her, you suddenly seized her by the hand with passion and, mounting her onto your chariot, carried her away; thereupon, a great roar of the enemies spread across the earth.
"Where has Paśupāla gone?"—with such cries, the kings, having waged war in anger against the Yadus, were defeated; yet you, O Lord, were not moved by them, like a lion by sycophantic dogs.

Thereafter, having disregarded the arrival of Rukmin in battle, he bound him, disfigured him, and then, his pride humbled, released him with words of encouragement; and together with his beloved Ramā, he returned to the city.

O Lord, you indeed delighted her at your ease in private— she whose mind was overcome with the shame of a new union, whose passion blossomed through the curiosity of love, and whose face shone with the rays of her laughter.
Thus experiencing delight day and night through various jests, you once again, O Straight-minded One,
stirred the extreme agitation of that fair-limbed woman with your crooked speech.
Then, delighting this beloved even more with superior skills of caressing, O Mukunda! as you recount your deeds to us, dispel our final suffering.
O Blessed One, you then requested from Satrājit the divine Syamantaka jewel which he had obtained like a hunter;
the reason for that surely appears manifold to me.
He intends to marry her daughter, who is devoted to you, under a pretext.
That excellent jewel was given to you by this small-minded man;
meanwhile, its brother Prasena, carrying it around his neck, went out hunting.
A lion killed him, mistaking the luster of the jewel for flesh.
The lord of monkeys, having slain him, gave the jewel as well to Bāla.
The people praised you, the stealer of the people's jewels, according to the words of Satrājit; for the nectar of the virtuous becomes a mere speck of fault [to others].
Therefore, even though you are omniscient, accompanied by your kinsmen, you were intent on seeking [the truth].
Having seen that Prasena, you also went to the cave of the monkey Hari.
Not reflecting upon your lordship, the aged Jāmbavān himself cried out, "Who here can restrain me who have taken refuge in Mukunda? and repeatedly shouted, "O All-pervading One!
O Lord of the Raghus! O Hari! Victory! Victory!"—no longer with mere fists, but with his entire being.
While wandering, that crest-jewel of devotees performed worship unto you.
Then, having understood this and accepting both the newly acquired jewel and the excellent gem given by him,
you went forth favoring him, and immediately bestowed the jewel upon Satrājit.
Thereupon, that wise king, overcome with shame, gave his daughter Bhāmā— whose eyes were tremulous— to you by word alone as if she were already bestowed upon another;
yet you, having approached her, have now rightfully won her along with the jewels.
With a joyful mind, Gahanāśaya took a jewel from him.
When you had departed for the Kurus with the story of the burning of the sons of Kuntī, Satyabhāmā— overcome with shame— was consoled by you; alas,
having been brought low by the words of Gāndinī’s son, Kṛtavarman!
Śatadhanu seized the jewel from Satrājit.
Seeing his beloved come to the Kurus out of grief,
they quickly killed Śatadhanvan and brought her back; then,
as if apprehensive regarding the jewel, they went to the house of the King of Mithilā.
Rāma thoroughly instructed the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra in the use of the mace.
O Blessed One, it was by Your very will that this Akrūra brought about the destruction of the wicked Satrājit;
yet You did not take back the jewel from Akrūra.
They say that it is for the purpose of bringing about prosperity for that very person.
O Lord, how has that son of Gāndinī, whose devotion to You was so exceedingly firm, come to possess such a mind set upon a wrong path?
He has become arrogant, thinking, "I am possessed of wisdom and tranquility."
You have surely acted to pacify pride.
Having called back Kṛtavarman, who had fled out of fear, and having displayed the jewel he had deposited there,
[Kṛṣṇa] was pleased to have placed it back in that very place, O bearer of the excellent bow.
O Lord of the Wind! May You, who lie between the breasts of Bhāmā, protect us.
Constantly caressing that Satyabhāmā, who was both affectionate and charming, he indeed went once more with her to the marriage of Yājñasenī;
for the sake of Pārtha’s pleasure, he again took up residence in Hastināpura.
O Lord! Having established the city of Śakraprastha, you have arrived.
When Bhadra— the younger sister of Bhava— was being sought by the Kaurava,
Śakrasūnu (Arjuna), disguised as a mendicant, carried her away at your word;
thereupon, pacifying the enraged Bala, he returned with him.
Accompanied by Satyabhāmā, he went to Śakraprastha, his dear friend, for the sake of joy.
There, even while sporting, you took up the Yamunā as she was seen on her bank and went to the city of Khāṇḍava, satisfying the fire-god;
O Lord, [you took] your father’s sister’s daughter, who was terrified of her brother and overcome by love.
In the midst of kings, you suddenly took delight in Mitravindā, the princess of Avanti.

O Lord! Having gone to Satyā and bound that daughter of Nagnajit as well as her seven excellent bulls in the twinkling of an eye, the seven-formed one [Viṣṇu] then gave her the name Bhadrā; and those [sages], headed by Santardana, bestowed it upon her.
O Giver of Boons, she is your sister; she is also your father's sister's daughter.
Even by the sons of Pṛthā and others, the target— a mere expanse of water where no fish could be caught—
was pierced; yet, having failed to win the Madraka maiden Śapharī, who was truly named for her mark,
you alone among them became the beloved of eight women.
You have heard from the words of the Lord of the Gods regarding the wicked deeds of the son of the Earth.
Mounted upon the best of birds that arrived as soon as it was remembered, you went to the enemy's city— carrying your beloved in your lap— as if to a pleasure grove,
shattering its fortresses with the sounds of your shattered armies and your incessant roars.
First, you turned the city of Prāgjyotiṣa into a pool of blood.
Mura, with five faces, leapt up from the midst of the ocean and its forests;
his head was swiftly split by you with your discus as he engaged in battle against four-tusked lordly elephants.
Having severed Naraka with his wheel, he made him cross over the ocean of hell.

Praised by the Earth, you immediately bestowed upon his son Bhagadatta a kingdom and an elephant, and dispatched the other elephants to your own city; yet sixteen more were sent by that rogue, whose mind was fixed on his own interests, to be bound there.
And he gave him thousands of women as well as a vast heap of wealth.
Having taken the earrings from Bhauma to give them to Aditi, he set out for heaven,
honored by Śakra and the other gods; together with his beloved, who was filled with longing among the celestial women,
he arrived after having angrily seized the Kalpa-tree and, having conquered Indra, approached him.
But you have composed this [work] precisely to explain that such is the fault of pride in one's own excellence.
Creating a wish-fulfilling tree in the courtyard of Satyabhāmā’s palace, He accepted sixteen thousand women and, assuming many forms in each house, delighted them with various pastimes;
thus, even in every single home, His diverse movements were beheld by Nārada as a marvel.
Furthermore, O Lord of the Abode of the Wind, protect us by producing ten sons in each of all [your wives]!

Pradyumna, the son of Rukmiṇī, was indeed a portion of yours; having been carried off by Śambara, he slew him and, together with Rati, returned to his own city and married the blessed daughter of Rukmin.
Then his son Aniruddha, a treasury of virtues, married Rocanā, the granddaughter of Rukmin.
There, having gone to the wedding, you were struck down by the wielder of the mace (Balarāma), while Rukmin was also slain due to the enmity arising from the gambling match.
This Uṣā, the highly honored daughter of Bāṇa, the son of Bali who possessed a thousand arms and was a devotee of Maheśvara,
has indeed never before seen this grandson of yours, Aniruddha.
O Blessed One! Having experienced this in a dream, she became afflicted by the pain of separation.
The yoginī Citralekhā is indeed exceedingly skillful; as she draws all the young men, her friend,
she recognizes Aniruddha there in the darkness of the night.
May he obtain [his desires] from your abode through the power of yoga.
While he was enjoying himself happily with his beloved in the inner apartments of the princess,
Śarva’s brother (Kṛṣṇa) somehow managed to bind him;
this was due to the intense wrath arising from the news concerning him, as reported by the venerable Nārada.
You besieged his city of Śoṇitapura with the Yadus.
The Lord of the city, the protector of Śailapriyā’s daughter and master of the Bhūtas, together with his hosts of spirits, fearlessly obstructed the Yadu army;
meanwhile, the mighty Bāṇa swiftly engaged Yuyudhāna in combat.
Guha joined with Pradyumna, while you, O destroyer of cities, were united with him as well.
When Giriśa had been rendered unconscious by your weapon, with all his other weapons neutralized,
the Bhūtas fled and the heroic Pramathas were crushed in terror;
then Skanda, along with his companion, the flower-arrowed god, leaped forward.
That kumbhāṇḍa quickly and forcefully shattered the vessel as if it were new.
When five hundred bows were forcibly brought forward, yet the arrows became useless as their strings were severed, the Lord of Fever approached at once and was instantly cured by your fever.
Then, having praised you and bestowed upon those who follow your conduct the state of being free from fever, that fever departed.
For generally, even those who possess inner knowledge are fierce and engage in terrible deeds due to the abundance of darkness.

As he brandished the arrow— terrible with its various weapons— and as it was about to strike again due to the fault of his pride, Śaṅkara, desiring to instantly awaken him whose faults were now entirely severed, sang this song;
by that speech, he who was dear to him became fearless on both sides, with only two arms remaining.
Having released him and being honored by him, you returned to your own city together with Aniruddha and Uṣā.

In the battle with Bāṇa here, he repeatedly defeated Śakra in the seizing of Nanda, Varuṇa in the leading away of children, Yama in the drinking of forest fires, Vāyu’s friend (Agni) in the consumption of fire, and Vidhi in the theft of his bull.
O All-pervading Lord! Thus, this incarnation of yours, which excels the entire universe, is victorious.

O Lord of the Wind! Protect me—you who, out of anger toward a twice-born, sent King Nṛga, who had assumed the body of a lizard, to the abode of the gods, while teaching your own people unsurpassed devotion to the twice-born.
Then, while Rāma had gone to Gokula and was intent upon women, and while [Kṛṣṇa],
blinded by pride, had been summoned but had not yet returned to subdue the Yamunā,
[Kaṃsa]— deluded by the words of his servants— began to act according to his own will.
Pauṇḍraka Vāsudeva dispatched a messenger to you.
"I am Nārāyaṇa, descended here upon this earth;
you indeed bear my very characteristics.
Cast them aside and come to me for refuge"—thus [he spoke] to you.
The messenger spoke while being laughed at by everyone in the assembly.
Then, when the messenger had departed, you, O Yadava soldier,
went forth and beheld the form of Pauṇḍraka; indeed,
upon his chest was a mark made by the heat [of the discus], which was of no small value.
Wearing the Śrīkaustubha gem, makara-shaped earrings, and yellow garments.
As he discharged his own Sudarśana discus made of black iron,
you severed his head with that Sudarśana which scattered masses of the fire of cosmic destruction, and you crushed his army.
And you made even the head of that friend, Kāśīpa, [to fall] in Kāśī.
For a long time, his mind was firmly fixed on the conviction that even by my dullness and the speech of a child, I alone am indeed Śrī Vāsudeva;
thus, through the thought of identity with you, he attained union (sāyujya).
Who indeed could know whose good deed it was, or how?
Then the son of the Lord of Kāśī, named Sudakṣiṇa,
having worshipped Śarva and performed a ritual for his own success,
created a certain fire of magic (*kṛtyā*) by means of which [the enemies] were terrified in the battle with Bāṇa.
He released [the arrow] toward him together with the beings who were somehow obstructing it.
O Lord! Even when pointed out by the terrified citizens who beheld a Kṛtyā— burning everything down with feet as tall as palm trees—
you did not stir from your gambling festival.
You swiftly cast away the Wheel of Time that was standing at your side.
When your great weapon of immeasurable splendor fell upon him,
the Ghorakṛtyā, alas, indeed fled crying "Hā! Hā!",
while he, Sudakṣiṇa, out of anger, acted with improper conduct.
He utterly consumed the wheel and burned down the city of Kāśī.
Indeed, that Vidura, having previously rendered assistance in the destruction of the Rākṣasas, then fell into wickedness in order to meet his death by a portion of you;
struck by the palm of the wielder of the plow while fighting, he truly fell down.

Seeking to pacify the Kurus, Rāma went to Sāmba, who was bound by the son of Kauravya for the abduction of the Kurus' daughter; he released him after the city had been uprooted by the elephants raised by the anger of that man's words.
At that time, you did not release the army of the Yadus, thinking they were to be slain by the sons of Pāṇḍu.
O Lord of the City of Wind! I serve you, whose play is difficult to comprehend, for the sake of quelling my suffering.

Then, at one time during an eclipse of the sun, you— having placed the sons of Kṛtavarman and Kāma in the city and surrounded by the women of the Yadu clan— arrived at the excellent sacred ford known as Samantapañcaka.
For the greater benefit of the multitude of people, you yourself again immersed yourself there in the waters of that sacred ford;
having relinquished heaps of wealth to the flocks of brahmins, you sought reconciliation with your friends, the Kurus, Pāṇḍavas, and others.
Indeed, the daughter of Drupada, together with her beloved women and burdened by a deep weight of devotion toward you,
rejoiced exceedingly along with those other ladies at the methods for bringing about your capture that they had devised.

And thereafter, O Blessed One, having observed the cowherd women and approached them out of great curiosity, you honored them and affectionately followed after those wives of the cattle-herders, whose limbs were marked by the distress of separation from you for so long.

And immediately, through the festival of beholding you, the hearts of those shapely women were stolen by pride; they cast off their bodices with excessive passion and sought your embrace upon breasts that were even more delightful for their familiarity.
"Because quarrels with my enemies have repeatedly approached me, such a long delay has occurred"—
as you spoke thus while embracing her, Rādhikā, truly overcome by intense passion, suddenly hid herself within you.
Then, having placed them in a secluded place and freed them from the pain of separation, you bestowed upon them the awakening to reality, saying:
"May it clearly arise in your minds that 'I am the Self, whose nature is consciousness and supreme bliss.'"

In the past, their separation was somewhat mitigated by the instructions of Uddhava, being mixed with the essence of happiness; but thereafter, for them, there arose a contemplation of You that consisted of supreme, singular bliss.
Then, as the multitudes of excellent sages were being asked by your father for auspicious rites to pacify his misfortunes,
he was made to desist even with broad laughter, as they said, "While you are present, what is the use of these other auspicious rites?"

While that great sacrifice was being performed and the circle of friends was filled with joy, the cowherds together enjoyed for three months the flavor of their attachment to you, honored by the people, just as they had before in the village.

At the time of departure, having come together and firmly embraced Rādhā, and seeing her free from distress, he departed for his city with a joyful heart; O Lord of Pavanapura, protect me from diseases!

Then, O Lord, for the sake of those who have no protector or refuge, you dispatched a certain person to the eighteen thousand million kings of the Magadha land, who had been afflicted by long-standing oppression.
He begged for nothing other than the mendicant's bowl; what was the use of saying more?

Desiring to go to Magadha, yet thereafter distressed by two tasks— the preparations for Yudhiṣṭhira’s sacrifice as uttered by Nārada and the sacrifice of one who had been defeated— Uddhava [concluded] that both objectives would be accomplished through the sacrifice of the one who was the adversary.
Having praised [him], he went together with his own people to the city of Yudhiṣṭhira.
When you, accompanied by your entire retinue of consorts, have arrived, Yudhiṣṭhira— having conquered the earth with his brothers who were nurtured by your sidelong glances—
bears incomparable glory, alas, acting like a servant to his devotees.
O noble lady! He has dispatched you to the King of Magadha along with Bhīma and Arjuna.
O King! Thereafter, you three went to the city of Girivraja and, under the guise of Brahmins, challenged that Māgadha to a festival of battle;
and by engaging him in combat, you caused him—who had not yet fully exhausted his merit—to be struck down by the son of the Wind.
Having observed this together with Jiṣṇu, you too stood ready for battle, O King.
Having struck down the son of Jaras— who was arrogant due to unceasing battles— with the signal of splitting the tree-branch, and having him torn apart by the wind-born [Hanuman],
he joyfully released the kings and favored them with supreme devotion.
And for the protection of the Dharma on earth, you dispatched [your disciples], even though they were free from desire.
Thereafter, when Yudhiṣṭhira was performing the Rājasūya sacrifice—
which was bustling with all the kings who had become contented servants—
you too, O Lord of the World, performed the washing of the feet of the twice-born and other such rites.
What more can be said? The rise in fortune of this best of kings is truly marvelous!
Then, having deliberated upon the procedure for the foremost worship during the sacrificial rite, that son of Dharma, following the words of Sahadeva,
joyfully performed the offering for the Soul of All Beings in the assembly.
Then, the entire abode, including its gods and humans, attained complete satisfaction.
Then, while the sages and kings stood by, the King of Cedi immediately exclaimed, "Alas! What fool would honor a mere boy who is a wicked, stubborn beast?
Thus, as he was spewing forth a torrent of such insults toward you from his seat—
Raising their weapons, the Pāṇḍavas rushed together and fell upon him.
Having warded off those on your own side, you alone shall strike off the head of the approaching enemy with your own weapon, the destroyer of demons;
for your pure intellect has been constantly purified by reflections gained through three previous births.
By you, he was brought to supreme oneness, a state difficult for yogis to attain.
Then, when that excellent sacrifice had been completed by you with great concentration, the people departed, exclaiming, "Victory to the son of Dharma! Victory to Kṛṣṇa!
But that wicked Suyodhana was shaken in spirit by the prosperity of his rival.
Offered at the entrance of the assembly hall by me, it caused confusion due to the delusion that it was land where there was water.
Then, O Lord, as You were sowing the seed for the immediate removal of the earth's burden, a certain smile arose from Drupada and Dhananjaya, manifesting through the play of their side-long glances.
O Janārdana, dweller in the city of the Maruts, protect me from disease!

At the wedding of Bhaiṣmī, Sālva, who had been defeated by the Yadu forces, obtained from the moon-crested Lord Śiva the Saubha aerial chariot; that master of illusion now dwells with you and has overwhelmed the Kurus and your city.
Pradyumna, of fierce valor, while checking him along with all the Yadu warriors, has captured him.
And a battle took place with his minister Dyumanta for twenty-seven days.
Just then, O Rāma, you arrived swiftly and hemmed in that lord of Saubha, whose army was nearly shattered; he indeed caused your Śārṅga bow to fall with his mace,
and even before your very eyes, he struck down your illusory father for half a moment.
"Some say it was not understood; Vyāsa himself forbade this contemptible view."
Having swiftly hurled Saubha into the ocean, crushed by his mace, and having cut down even Śālva with his discus,
Dantavakra rushed forward impetuously and released his mace at you;
struck by the Kaumodakī, he too— though a treasury of merit— attained oneness [with the Divine] like Caidya.
This incarnation was undertaken for the sake of liberating all those who have previously fixed their minds upon you.
Then, when you had arrived and the gambling match had begun in the assembly of the Kurus,

you fashioned for the weeping Yājñasenī— held in captivity— an endless garland of raiment; thereafter, she was protected by the thought of Draupadī, who was terrified by the sage who was a portion of Śarva born from the end of the food.
Having arrived at the edge of the forest, you satisfied the assembly of sages by eating only vegetables.

Then, while the deliberations for the preparations of war were being held, you alone, chosen by Phalguna and granted an army, went as an envoy to the city of the Kauravas for the sake of the Pandavas;
yet, when your words— held in high esteem by Bhishma, Drona, and others— were indeed reviled by the Kaurava, [the battle began].
Revealing your universal form, you arrived after having shaken the city within the assembly of sages.

O Kṛṣṇa, you were indeed the charioteer for the victorious Arjuna at the front of the battle; seeing that hero distressed and compassionate toward the slaughter of his kin, you said to him: "Alas, my friend! This self (ātman) is eternal and one.
Who here is to be slain, and who is the slayer? Therefore, casting aside the fear of death, offer yourself to Me."
He engages in righteous battle, displaying his universal form by leading his nature astray.
Then, while Bhīṣma— the crest-jewel of devotees— was constantly intent on the sole task of relieving the earth’s burden,
and while Arjuna was perpetually piercing thousands of mountains and had become weary;
[Arjuna], filled with wrath, abandoned his vow of being unarmed and seized the preeminent enemy.
Then, seeing him running toward you with palms joined and head bowed, you departed out of joy.

In that battle, while the Vaiṣṇava weapon discharged by Bhagadatta— whose elephant was steady on the battlefield— struck Droṇa’s chest, Arjuna, his splendor eclipsing the sun with his discus, crushed the King of Sindhu;
and when Karṇa released the Nāga weapon, he merely caused the earth to bow down, leaving the king with his crown severed.
In every instance there, O Pārtha, what indeed have you not done for the sake of the Pāṇḍavas?

At the start of the battle, that wielder of the plow indeed went to the sacred ford; while traveling toward the Naimiṣa forest, he brought about the destruction of those who did not rise to greet him during a period of birth-impurity.
Then, having appointed his son to that position, he crushed Balvala—the destroyer of sacrifices—on the day of the full moon, and at the end of the combat, he bathed at the sacred ford.
Having witnessed the lack of peace in the battle between Bhīma and Duryodhana, he has arrived and gone to your city.

Approaching the son of Droṇa, whose intellect was destroyed by the slaying of the sleeping sons of Draupadī, Vijaya (Arjuna) neutralized that discharged Brahmā-missile with your words and seized his crest-jewel;
furthermore, for the destruction of the Pāṇḍavas, he cast that missile again into the womb of Uttarā.
O All-pervading Lord, it is said that while protecting [the world], Cakrapāṇi entered the belly as one whose size is merely that of a thumb!
Having proclaimed the entire flood of Dharma to the Son of Dharma (Yudhiṣṭhira), Bhīṣma— whose death was subject to his own will—
attained the state of the partless Brahman (*niṣkalabrahmabhūya*) the very moment he beheld you with the fullness of devotion.
Then, having performed three most magnificent horse-sacrifices for the Son of Dharma, whose desires were now fulfilled, [he departed].
O Lord of the City of Wind! You have arrived at Dvārakā; protect me from all diseases!

A brahmin named Kucela, who had become your fellow student, spent his days as a tranquil householder in the home of Sāndīpani; free from desire for wealth and other such things, he lived with single-minded devotion to you alone.
Then his beloved wife, who shared his very same character, likewise addressed our horse-like mind:
"O, why is the Lord of Ramā, our friend, not served for the sake of obtaining a livelihood?"
Thus addressed by his beloved, who was afflicted by hunger, he— though feeling disdain for wealth that brings intoxication—
then departed, carrying the *pṛthuka* grains as a gift tucked within the hem of his garment out of curiosity to behold you.
Having gone to your wondrous city and reached the palace of Śaibyā among the houses, he entered it as if it were Vaikuṇṭha and found bliss; how much more so, then, through your own great honor?
Held in your hand by your beloved and fanned by her, you spoke of what had been done in the past:
how, urged by your teacher’s wife, you had endured a rain out of season in the forest for the sake of fuel.

Then, as you were about to seize the flat rice from this child who was fond of traps, and had already taken a single mouthful into your fist, Ramā, approaching in haste, indeed grasped your hand, saying, "Enough, enough! Surely this much is sufficient."

Honored by you with devotion while dwelling in the city for a single night among your devotees with great happiness, alas, on the following day he departed without wealth; truly, your grace is of wondrous form!
For had Acyuta not given it when I requested it, would he have said, "Tell me what [else] you want," as he was departing?
With his mind immersed in the play of your smile and speech, he then gradually beheld the palace radiant with jewels.

Wandering for a moment, wondering if he had lost his way, he entered his home and beheld his beloved, surrounded by her friends and adorned with jewels and gold; and he realized that this was the great miracle of your compassion.
Though dwelling within the halls of jewels, he himself attained immortality through the weight of his own surging devotion;
O Lord of Marutpura, you who thus fulfill the desires of your devotees, take away my diseases!

Long ago, having heard of the death of Ācārya’s sons, your mother Utkalī, longing for a sight of her own six children, obtained an offering on the ground where her son had been born; by that [offering] you were honored. Due to the curse of the Creator, you became the son of Kaśipu, who was possessed of gold, and were crushed by Kaṃsa, the son of Śūri.
Having brought them here and shown them to me, you did not lead these former sons of Marīci back to their own abode.
Desiring to bestow grace simultaneously upon the lord of brahmins named Śrutadeva and upon King Bahulāśva, who was filled with devotion,
you arrived at Mithilā accompanied by ascetics.
Moving with a dual form simultaneously to the abodes of both, he performed worship with abundant riches by one [form],
and with fruits, boiled rice, and other offerings gathered on that very day by the other.
You bestowed your favor equally upon these two and granted them liberation.
Furthermore, in Dvārakā, you spoke of the death of the Brahmin’s son and his lamentations,

saying, "Who indeed can thwart destiny?"— for even he who bears the universe could not endure it; and thus, in order to humble the pride of Arjuna and to blunt his intellect which was obstructed by its human perception of you, [you acted].
I believe it is for the purpose of establishing [the mind] upon reality by means of beholding the supreme state.
His eight sons were lost once again through your neglect; thus, O Lord of Dvārakā, a harsh reproach became clear to the people.
Then, at that opportune moment, Pārtha dwelt there out of friendship, and during the birth of his ninth son, he heard the lamentation of the eminent brāhmaṇa.
Having heard this, he made a vow: "If my son is not brought back, I shall enter the fire."
Proudly, he went to the abode of the twice-born without asking you; obstructing the birth-chamber with nets of arrows and great missiles while the prince was suddenly seen and then vanished again,
he reached the southern, northern, and other cities of the foremost gods by means of his magic science.
As he was about to fall into the fire with his efforts rendered futile, you stopped him with a smile.

Together with him, he set out toward the western direction on that exceedingly swift chariot; having passed beyond the Lokāloka mountain, he then shrouded the mass of darkness with the splendor of his discus.
Then, seeing Vijaya standing there, his vision obscured by the rays of the discus, [the Lord] called out repeatedly, "Look! Look! to the people.
On the further shore, you have indeed set foot in a place far, far beyond all darkness.
There he sat upon the couch of the lord of serpents, adorned with divine ornaments and weapons, wearing yellow garments, his glorious body dark as a fresh rain-cloud;
the sovereign of the three forms, the single ultimate purpose of the three Vedas.
O Supreme Self! Accompanied by your dear friend, you alone have assumed this form of peace.
"O youths, I myself have brought these sons of the twice-born here so that you two might behold them clearly, though they were previously divided by being either manifest or hidden; indeed,
I have delivered them back to you once again."
The sons of Pāṇḍu, whose greatness was celebrated by the twice-born, were heirs to no other inheritance.
Thus, delighting the world with various pastimes, nourishing the Vṛṣṇi clan,
performing diverse sacrifices with incomparable enjoyments, and pleasing the deer-eyed women,
he descended under the pretext of removing the earth's burden in order to liberate those who take refuge at his lotus feet.
You, who are none other than the manifest, perfect Brahman, appeared among the Yadus, assuming the form of a human being.
Generally, O compassionate one, Nārada was not present in Dvāravatī; for he, whose heart was moistened by the nectar of your love,
attained the realization of ultimate truth from you at one time— your father, who was indeed a treasure-house of merit—
and likewise the wise Uddhava, the foremost among devotees, received it from you alone.
Having attained the essence of consciousness, that person indeed now dwells in Badarī for the welfare of the world.
Victorious is this incarnation as Kṛṣṇa of yours, O All-pervading Lord! Through various yogic means— such as friendship, fear, affection, hatred, and passion— which are beyond compare and effortless,
all people everywhere have crossed over every affliction and attained the state of immortality.
Therefore, O Lord of the City of Wind, may you exist for the pacification of all afflictions and for the fulfillment of devotion.

O Knower of Ramā! I know that if worldly power were not immediately attainable for Your devotees here, You would first bring about the pacification of those who are devoid of self-restraint by destroying their pride,
and only then bestow every desire.
Indeed, among those who are thus tranquil, there is certainly no talk of passing away.
O Lord! Alas, how painful it is that some, while worshipping Brahmā, Śiva, and others— who are instantly appeased yet easily provoked— according to their own merits,
fall away due to a lack of long-term vision.
Indeed, the example of the wolf and the deer in this case is quite clear.
For once, that son of Śakuni, having quickly satisfied the Lord Nārada, asked him [for a boon];
and he directed him to worship the Lord of the Mountain (Śiva), but not you, who are a kinsman to the wicked and devoid of merit.
Having performed severe austerities, he indeed became enraged; on the seventh day,
having severed his head and immediately presented it before the Destroyer of Cities (Śiva),
he brought about his own destruction by offering that exceedingly small and fierce head as a tribute.
From Jagannātha he chose [this boon]: "Where is the burden of auspiciousness for those who are turned away from you?"
Then, like a lord of deer fleeing from a hunter, he rushed toward Rudra, the deliverer who is himself liberated from bondage;
yet the god, out of fear of the demon, turned in every direction,
casting his gaze behind him while all the worlds remained silent as they beheld Śarva about to step upon his foot.
From afar, you stood before the Dānava in the form of a clever young boy.
"Blessings to you, O son of a bird! Why do you wander about now? If you have doubt regarding my words because of the speech of a *piśāca*, why, my dear, do you not place your finger upon your head?
Thus, bewildered by your words, he placed his hand upon his head and fell down with a crash.
For even the downfall of one who worships another, and even the destiny of Śiva himself, is indeed you alone.
It is said that the ascetics dwelling near the Sarasvatī river directed Bhṛgu to determine which of the three forms possessed the greatest essence;
yet this [form], because of its disregard for the Creator who had arisen with obstructed wrath, [remained superior].
And even when you desired to kill Hara, [the weapon] went to you when it was held by Girijā.
O best of sages, when you were sleeping on the lap of Ramā with eyes like lotuses and a Brahmin was joyfully striking you with his foot, you rose up;
may you always forgive all this for me.
"You have declared that the mark of your foot is the ornament here."
Having become firmly resolved and having bound their hearts to you,
those excellent sages of the Sarasvatī have attained liberation;
for you, O Acyuta, are thus free from the defect of falling away again.
We worship only that single body which is the accumulation of all sentient beings.

O Viṣṇu! At the beginning of the creation of the world, You—who possess a non-dual form of pure existence, consciousness, and supreme bliss—were praised by multitudes of Vedas like bards; O Infinite One!
You are the Supreme Self, the mass of good fortune for the liberation of bound souls.
O dweller in the city of the Wind! I resort to you for the sake of dispelling fatigue and exhaustion.
O Supreme Self! Your greatness—which is victorious over Śarva and all others—is established here in the lives of Vṛka, Bhṛgu, Suni, Mohinī, Ambarīṣa, and others;
it remains undivided from the partless [Absolute], yet manifest as the immanent.
Whatever appears at all is indeed Your own form.
Regarding that group of five, beginning with Sadāśiva, who is the Lord of the three forms— of which they say Sadāśiva is indeed the very body of the Supreme Self—
you alone are that Īśvara therein, residing in the realm of Vikuṇṭha.
Furthermore, you partake in the state of threefoldness within the three divisions of the realm of truth.

Even there, they say that Viṣṇu is your body composed of *sattva*; Brahmā, however, is thin in *sattva* and filled with *rajas* alone; yet even in him, there exists an intensity of *sattva* which is a transformation of *tamas*.
And [this] movement and so forth belong to your form bearing the name Śaṅkara.
And they indeed praise you, the primordial person who transcends the three forms,
even as Śarva, for the sake of your being composed of all things; yet,
in the ritual of worship, they do so by your own nature.
The statement "it is your form" is for us an exceedingly firm and abundant means of valid cognition.
Even the Lord Śrī Śaṅkara honors you alone among all things— he who is indeed free from partiality—
for he [composed] the *Sahasranāma* and other works centered solely upon you.
He explained [the scriptures] while being intent on praising you, and at the end, he attained the supreme state.
And he spoke of you, the Lord of all, who transcends the three forms and is as beautiful as a kalāya seed at the beginning of the mantra scriptures;
indeed, having described the meditation on the partless [aspect] within the *praṇava*.
There he spoke of you alone as the All, and no other.
In the *Samastasāra* and the *Purāṇasaṃgraha*, your majesty alone is described without any doubt;
yet, from the third part of the true state associated with the three forms, the supreme state of you, the Wielder of the Trident, has not been told.
O Lord! That form which was revealed here in the Brahma-kalpa for the sake of the Creator, as described in the second book of the Bhāgavata, You called by the names Hari and Śarva.
Even one devoted to Śiva [should worship] the illustrious Mādhava in the *Purāṇasāra*.
For those who worship Giriśa in accordance with their own innate nature,
the fruit indeed arises from their firm devotion to Him; for Vyāsa composed this work for the sake of such qualified aspirants.
In the *Skandapurāṇa* and other texts, the statements regarding your defeat are merely arthavādas.
The proclamation of the true meaning, restatement, and contradictory discourse— these three modes of explanatory discourse (arthavāda) indeed serve the purpose of persuasion.
In the *Skandha* and other such works, there are many such contradictory discourses here.
These include self-conceit, contempt for others, and the practice of [insulting] them.
O All-pervading Lord! Whatever has been spoken by me, though ignorant, has indeed been observed through the words of the mantra scriptures and other sources;
O You who are praised in the Bhāgavata, which contains the essence of Vyāsa’s utterances!
Shake off the afflictions and offer a weight of devotion, O Supreme Self!

O Śrī Kṛṣṇa! I consider the worship of Your feet to be the most fearless refuge for a distressed mortal whose vision is bound by false objects; for through it, the fear of one who stands upon the path of delusion while established in the rules of devotion ordained by You entirely departs, as You are the Self of all.
O God of gods, Soul of all! Even while running with eyes closed, one does not stumble anywhere.
O Infinite One! Whatever I do here with body, speech, or even mind, my self being impelled by Your power—I offer all that here unto You, the Supreme.
Even one who is by birth a dog-cooker (outcaste), if his mind, actions, speech, senses, and objects are dedicated to You—
The vital breath purifies the entire universe, yet not so for one whose mind is turned away from Your feet, O best of Brahmins.
Fear indeed arises from a second; and the second is surely imagined by the mind.
Therefore, one who is habituated to the practice of unity should restrain the heart here with the intellect according to one's ability.
When that [second] is pierced by *māyā*, it no longer appears as such to the Lord of Māyā.
Therefore, O Lord, by constantly worshipping you with great devotion, may I abandon all fear.

The arising and growth of devotion for those who dwell at Your feet are attained only through association with You, just as prosperity in this world comes to the fortunate through association with the wealthy. Therefore,
O Lord, may I indeed have constant association with them, so that from their mouths [may arise] the blossoming of wisdom...
And through the various modes of your majesty, devotion—purified of sin—becomes exceedingly firm.
With great devotion toward the paths to the highest good, repeatedly singing of his births and deeds, and chanting his auspicious names, his soul runs forth in both directions;
sometimes with a rising smile, sometimes weeping, and at other times roaring as he sings aloud.
O Mother, dancing like one possessed by madness, have mercy so that I may move as one excluded from the world.
All these beings, though composed of the elements, as well as birds, fish, wild animals,
mortals, friends, and even enemies— I, whose mind is restrained, perceive them all as consisting of You and as being bowed in reverence to You.
For by Your grace, through service to You, may there arise in me firm devotion and detachment, whereby I may attain perfection.
And even the realization of Your true nature, O Lord of the World, occurs without any effort or distinction.
May I not be deluded by hunger, thirst, and other afflictions born of the path of worldly existence, for my mind is absorbed in You;
may I possess constant mindfulness, remaining unshakable from Your feet even for a moment’s duration;
and, through the realization of its illusory nature, may I be free from both joy and distress regarding the desirable and the undesirable.
May I move about with a soul made even more cooled by the moonlight of your toenails.
If you have no further authority now for me to attain the realization of my oneness with these beings,
then let there be love for You, friendship for You, compassion for those of dull intellect, and equanimity toward Your enemies;
or else, let my curiosity for worshiping Your image increase through most profound faith.
Nevertheless, one who serves you quickly attains the state of being the most excellent among devotees.

O Lord of the World! May Your Māyā—which, concealing Your true nature, manifests as earth, water, wind, and so forth; which casts living beings—whose movements are rendered helpless by the weight of their vast accumulation of karma—into the snare of suffering—not overcome me. O Mother, may it be employed for its own pacification.
"O Lord! Only devotion to Your feet," thus spoke the awakened Siddhayogin, O Compassionate One!

Having fully awakened my discernment by beholding the sufferings of living beings, and having obtained from the most excellent of teachers the reality of your nature— along with an abundance of devotion arising from the stories of your qualities and deeds—
I shall cross over this illusion and rejoice in your state, which consists of supreme bliss.
O Lord of the City of Wind! May this preliminary rite destroy all diseases.

O Lord! Having understood that all actions have been described by the Vedas as being devoid of attachment to their fruits, you indeed practice them only after offering them unto Me; through this, you attain the state of actionlessness (naiṣkarmya).
Let there never be the engagement of mind, action, or speech in anything whatsoever that is prohibited by the Vedas.
Even if that which is difficult to avoid has been attained, it indeed becomes offered within the radiance of consciousness.
But as for another who is devoted to the path of action, he should meditate upon the desired form— charming and consisting of pure goodness— whether in stone, in his heart,
or in clay; and with flowers, modest offerings, and whatever else is prepared according to his ability, purified by devotion—
O Lord, performing worship that is ever excellent, may I enjoy Your grace!
Let women and Śūdras remain as they are, for they are worthy of your compassion, being deprived of hearing your stories and the like;
but alas, I grieve for those born into the families of the twice-born who have approached your feet yet remain unpeaceful,
performing sacrifices for the sake of a livelihood while failing to listen to you, even though you have been described so many times.
What will those who are arrogant because of their learning and noble birth not do? Do not treat me in such a manner.

"O Kṛṣṇa! This wicked man calls out 'Rāma' in order to conceal his own conduct; the words of this shameless one have prevented me from saying much more. My brother, it is said, is of barren character and always worships Viṣṇu"—thus you speak to those who are wise.
They revile you and laugh aloud at those who have placed their affection in you; do not make me such as they.
In the Kṛta age, they delight in you, who possess the body of the best of sages and have a white radiance, through their ascetic penances;
in the Tretā age, they worship you in the form of sacrifice, with a reddish body marked by the sacrificial ladle (sruk) and spoon (sruva);
and in the Dvāpara age, they serve you, whose limbs are dark-blue, as you sport with the mace that slays enemies, according to the paths of Tantra.
In this age of Kali, human beings worship you, the Blue One, through congregational chanting and other such means.
Victorious is this Kali age, O enemy of Mura! For in it, O Lord of all, people attain Your grace in no long time through the very paths of congregational chanting and other such practices.
Indeed, those who were born in the Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kṛta ages now truly desire to be born in the Kali age.
O Lord! Do not deceive yourself by means of the poisonous juices of sense-objects regarding those very things that were born to you by fate.
In the Kali age, devotees will indeed abound in the land of Dravida; and there, by the Kāverī, the Tāmraparṇī, and the holy Kṛtamālā flowing westward, they shall flourish greatly.
O Lord! Alas, even for me, who am born within this very region, grant some taste of the essence of consciousness!
O Blessed One! Do not cause me to wander, bound by the nooses of desire; fulfill my service to You.

Having previously seen that enemy of Dharma, Kali, who is devoid of compassion, King Parīkṣit—though he drew his sword to slay him—did not strike him, for he was a knower of the essence of the *muni* [sages] due to his discernment (*sāra*).
Service to you is quickly accomplished here; it is not so with others, for this Kali is afraid of one devoted to you.
But as for that which has already been carried away by diseases and the like even before [this instruction], there—alas!—instruct him.
O Supreme Person! In this age of Kali, these eight— Gaṅgā, Gītā, Gāyatrī, Tulasī, Gopīcandana,
the worship of the Sālagrāma, the Ekādaśī fast, and the syllables of Your name—
